Improving on a timeless recipe

@media screen and (max-width: 767px) {
}

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by Paul de Casteljau in 1959, and refined by Pierre Bézier in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and
new ones continue to be proposed, these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

Source

Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka lerps) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\begin{array}{ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&& ... &&&&&& ... \\
\end{array}
$$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier spline, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is completely wrong, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a curvature comb which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite mean: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments

When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \mathbf{T}\left(t\right) = \frac{\displaystyle \gamma'\left(t\right)}{\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\mathbf{K}\left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \mathbf{K}\left(t\right) = \mathbf{T}\left(t\right) \times \frac{\gamma''\left(t\right)}{|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \mathbf{T}\left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\mathbf{K}\left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{T}\left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\mathbf{K}\left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\mathbf{K}\left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\begin{cases}
a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\end{cases}
$$

Where:

$$
\begin{array}{lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\mathbf{T}(0) \times \mathbf{T}(1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\mathbf{T}(0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\mathbf{T}(1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\end{array}
$$

This captures a few things:

The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.

The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.

The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\mathbf{T_i}$. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \frac{\displaystyle -a_0 \cdot l_0^2 - c_0}{\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \frac{\displaystyle -a_1 \cdot l_1^2 - c_1}{\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle -b \cdot l_0 - c_1}{\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle -b \cdot l_1 - c_0}{\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\mathbf{g_0} = \begin{bmatrix}2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\end{bmatrix} \\[0.3em]
\mathbf{g_1} = \begin{bmatrix}b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \frac{\displaystyle \mathbf{g_0} \cdot \mathbf{g_1}}{\displaystyle |\mathbf{g_0}||\mathbf{g_1}|}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\mathbf{l}|$ i.e. $\sqrt{l_0^2 + l_1^2}$, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
w_{heuristic}\left(\mathbf{l}\right) = \left(\frac{\displaystyle l_0 \cdot l_1 \cdot \arccos\left(-\cos \theta\right)}{\displaystyle |\mathbf{l}|^2}\right)^2
$$

Large $|\mathbf{l}|$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option

When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
w_{sample}\left(\mathbf{l}\right) = \frac{1}{|\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{l}_{average}|^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on GitLab.

Conceived by Paul de Casteljau in 1959, and refined by Pierre Bézier in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. title: The Ceaseless Ceasefire
subtitle: All across the world, people are trapped by forces far beyond their control.

articleBody:
All across the world, people are trapped by forces far beyond their control. Handcuffed by situations which they are powerless to change.

I spent countless hours talking to people like this from Southeast Asia to North Africa. Their immediate circumstances couldn’t have been more different. They hailed from radically dissimilar backgrounds; they were of different races, ethnicities, and religions. But they were bound together by one unifying force: organized, armed violence. Or, rather, the imposition of it upon them. These people were just living their lives when war arrived on their doorsteps.

When most people think of war, they think of armed soldiers. But I think of grandmothers and toddlers. Modern war zones are much more the province of civilians than combatants, even if the traditional “battlefield” has made a significant reappearance this century. Soldiers die. Civilians die in droves. Soldiers deploy here and there. Civilians are put to flight, en masse, often again and again. When memories of war invade my thoughts, I remember the tween whose hand was cut off, the farmer who dug his own grave and survived his execution, the paralyzed man who had to be left behind as troops attacked the village, the 2-year-old who survived a machete attack. Since World War II, such innocents have overwhelmingly been the main victims of armed conflict.

Being a war reporter taught me that ordinary people have extraordinary capabilities. I found that people the world over had the capacity to endure the unbearable and the survive the unthinkable. What they often cannot do, however, is push back on the source of their oppression and suffering. People can run from soldiers, but they cannot outrun war. The “safety” of a refugee camp is still an extension of the war zone. You can flee violence but still remain trapped by conflict.

Today, in her inaugural article for TomDispatch, Safia Southey — an international lawyer and expert on how societies reckon with wartime abuses — examines the plight of Palestinians in Gaza imprisoned by a conflict that refuses to die, the truce ostensively meant to save them, and the outside authorities that have trapped them in this “zombie conflict.” In this singular piece, Southey offers a window into the perverse mechanics of this ceaseless ceasefire cycle and what it would take to break it.

—Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

A Twilight Zone Between War and Peace

Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family spent the first anniversary of the Gaza ceasefire last month in a shelter they built from the debris of their own home. Ne’man Abu Jarad and his five daughters spent it in tents, still displaced and with no clear way back. These families and millions of other Palestinians find themselves in a twilight state between war and peace: a zombie conflict in which a ceasefire has been announced while Israeli military control and attacks continue. The agreement risks making that condition permanent by leaving Palestinian governance and Israeli withdrawal dependent on decisions made largely by outside powers.

For these families, whose circumstances were reported by the Associated Press, and others in their position, the ceasefire that was supposed to end the war has brought little control over what happens next. Whether they can return home, rebuild, or resume anything resembling ordinary life remains subject to decisions made by outside authorities, whose hold on Gaza’s future may be further entrenched by the agreement itself.

Related

Congress Might Sneakily Use Lame Duck to Deeply Intertwine the U.S. and Israeli Militaries

While violations of the ceasefire warrant the attention they receive (and more), the agreement’s own terms demand scrutiny too, since arrangements negotiated to end wars also decide who holds power once the fighting stops. Christine Bell, a legal scholar specializing in peace accords, has shown how such agreements can perform constitutional functions. They determine who governs, over what territory, and subject to whose approval.

In Gaza, the conditions for Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian self-government give outside actors considerable power to determine when, and whether, the transition ends. The framework therefore threatens to turn the temporary administration of a devastated territory into a durable system of external control with no enforceable end, legitimized by the very agreement meant to bring peace.

A Long History of Outside Control

Gaza’s current predicament has a long history of displacement and outside control. In 1947, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a plan to partition Palestine (then under British rule) into Arab and Jewish states. While Jewish leadership accepted the plan, Arab leadership rejected it. During the war surrounding Israel’s establishment in 1948, approximately 750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes. Many sought refuge in Gaza. The mass displacement and dispossession of the Nakba — Arabic for “catastrophe” — never ended.

Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in 1967. In 2005, it removed its settlements and withdrew its army from inside Gaza while retaining control over its airspace and maritime access and substantial authority over its borders and the movement of people and goods. In 2024, the International Court of Justice concluded that because Israel continued to exercise authority over Gaza’s borders and the movement of people and goods, the withdrawal had not entirely released it from its obligations under the law of occupation.

The current institution of Palestinian self-governance also began as a temporary arrangement intended to last no more than five years. The Oslo process of the 1990s provided for an interim Palestinian government in Gaza and the West Bank until a permanent settlement could be reached. That institution, the Palestinian Authority, remains central to proposals for Gaza’s future.

Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections and took control of Gaza in 2007 after armed conflict with Fatah, the rival Palestinian faction. Israel, citing security concerns, tightened its border restrictions into a blockade by land, sea, and air, restricting the movement of people into and out of Gaza and the entry of food, construction materials, and other necessities. Egypt restricted passage through its own border crossing. Years before the current war, the U.N.’s humanitarian office documented the effects: restrictions on movement and trade had undermined Gaza’s economy, increased its dependence on aid, and obstructed access to healthcare and education.

Related

What American Doctors Saw in Gaza

On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led groups attacked Israel, deliberately killing civilians and taking hostages; Human Rights Watch has documented these acts as crimes against humanity and war crimes. Israel’s subsequent military response devastated Gaza. By Oct. 21 of this year, Gaza’s Health Ministry reported 74,494 Palestinians killed and 175,604 injured. In an October 2026 report, the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and forces continued committing genocidal acts against Palestinians in Gaza after the ceasefire, with the intent to destroy the group in whole or in part. By September of this year, Israeli military control had expanded beyond the approximately 53 percent of Gaza envisioned under the ceasefire agreement to at least 60 percent.

From Resolution 2735 to Resolution 2803

In June 2024, the U.N. Security Council endorsed a three-phase framework in Resolution 2735. An initial ceasefire and exchanges of hostages and prisoners were to lead, upon agreement, to a permanent end to hostilities and full Israeli withdrawal, followed by major reconstruction. The initial ceasefire was to continue for as long as negotiations over the second phase went on.

Related

The Performative Ceasefire in Gaza

In November 2025, the Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza conflict and authorizing international arrangements for its implementation. The framework retains the language of transition while placing Gaza’s administration and redevelopment under the oversight of a Board of Peace chaired by Trump. Palestinian Authority control would depend on completing a reform program and demonstrating the capacity to govern securely and effectively. The resolution refers to earlier proposals, including a Saudi and French initiative calling for reforms to governance, transparency, public finances, and service provision. Israeli withdrawal is tied to demilitarization milestones to be agreed among the Israeli military, an International Stabilization Force, the guarantor states, and the United States. The force’s mandate includes demilitarization and civilian protection. An Israeli military presence along Gaza’s perimeter could remain until the territory is judged secure against a renewed terrorist threat.

The plan endorsed by the resolution states that Israel will not occupy or annex Gaza, that no one will be forced to leave, and that full humanitarian aid will enter immediately. Continued attacks and restrictions on assistance must therefore be assessed against those obligations, but compliance with these provisions would still not resolve the deeper problem. The framework grants outside institutions concrete powers over Gaza while making the restoration of Palestinian political authority dependent on future conditions. It establishes who governs during the transition far more clearly than it establishes how the transition ends.

The resolution authorizes the international arrangements until Dec. 31, 2027, subject to further Security Council action, but it sets no deadline for full Israeli military withdrawal or the transfer of political authority to Palestinians.

Who Decides When Gaza Is Secure?

Israeli withdrawal depends on milestones agreed with Israel and other actors, but the criteria for determining when those milestones have been satisfied, and the consequences of disagreement, remain ill defined. Whoever can set the benchmarks, withhold agreement, or dispute compliance has considerable power over how long Gaza remains under outside supervision. This effectively means that the decision will be made in large part by Israel and institutions overseeing the transition, including Trump’s Board of Peace, which counts Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a member.

No security arrangement can eliminate every future threat; clear benchmarks and a truly independent arbiter are essential if the ceasefire is to ever become a lasting peace.

The demand for protection against another attack is understandable. Hamas’s weapons, and its coercive power over Palestinians, are serious problems. But if the security conditions for withdrawal can be revised indefinitely, Palestinians cannot know when the promised transfer of authority will occur. The obligations of one armed faction should not determine whether an entire population has a political future.

Israel Policy Forum, a U.S. policy organization supporting a two-state solution, analyzed and supported the basic approach of the July 2026 road map. The proposal linked phased Hamas disarmament to incremental Israeli withdrawal and the creation of a new Palestinian civilian administration. The organization’s analysis described Israel’s refusal to accept that bargain, conflicting explanations of when withdrawal could proceed, and unresolved definitions and verification arrangements.

No security arrangement can eliminate every future threat; clear benchmarks and a truly independent arbiter are essential if the ceasefire is to ever become a lasting peace. Otherwise, the conditions for withdrawal could be extended indefinitely. If Hamas disarms and the promised withdrawal never comes, the disarmament stands while Israel’s commitment remains open to renegotiation. A single attack by a faction opposed to the agreement could then be invoked to suspend the political future of an entire population, allowing armed spoilers to trigger further delays in Palestinian self-government and giving Israel and the United States grounds to prolong those delays.

Related

No One Will Be Celebrating the 25th Anniversary of the Oslo Accords

Palestinians have seen an interim arrangement outlast its deadline before. The 1993 Oslo agreement between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization established a framework for interim Palestinian self-government and negotiations toward a permanent settlement. It envisioned a transitional period of no more than five years, with negotiations on permanent status to address the sovereignty and governance of Jerusalem, the fate of Palestinian refugees since 1948, Israeli settlements, and state borders. More than three decades later, there is still no comprehensive settlement. The new plan follows the same design: concrete authority now, political rights later.

The Cost of Delay

In an Oct. 2 report, the UN’s humanitarian office identified 217 displacement sites at medium to high risk of flooding, hosting approximately 235,000 people. Nearly 44,000 people were sheltering in unsafe buildings that required full or partial demolition, the report said. Restrictions on land access and on the entry of supplies continued to hamper preparations for winter.

Read Our Complete Coverage

TomDispatch

No later breakthrough can give back a lost winter, a child’s interrupted schooling, or a patient’s postponed treatment. The longer a household has to survive elsewhere, the harder it may become to rebuild the life it was forced to leave, and an agreement can keep promising recovery while the conditions for recovery disappear.

“The Trillion Dollar War Machine” by William D. Hartung and Ben Freeman. Available on Bookshop.org

Palestinians are also asked to prove they can govern before they are allowed to do so, and governing requires revenue. In the October report, the U.N. described how Israel’s withholding of approximately $6 billion in tax revenues it collected on the Palestinian Authority’s behalf was undermining that government body’s ability to provide services and pay salaries. The crisis extends beyond Gaza and exposes a circular test of readiness. An administration deprived of its own revenue struggles to deliver services, and those failures can then be invoked to justify continued outside supervision.

Blame works the same way: If a Palestinian administration is responsible for public services while other actors control access, security, and funding, residents may blame its officials for failures it could not prevent. The resulting loss of public trust would make representative government harder to build, and that weakness could in turn be cited as a reason for continued outside supervision.

Nathan J. Brown, a scholar of Palestinian politics, has argued that Gaza diplomacy is separating administrative functions from national political representation. A committee of technocrats can run clinics and restore water service, but deciding the political future of the people it serves requires authority grounded in their consent. An administration accountable primarily to a foreign board chaired by Trump lacks that democratic mandate.

The Role of Outside Powers

The United States helped broker the Gaza ceasefire, holds a central position in the system meant to implement it, and underwrites Israeli military power. According to the Congressional Research Service, the 2016 memorandum covering fiscal years 2019 through 2028 pledged $38 billion in military assistance, subject to congressional appropriation. Without credible American consequences for obstructing withdrawal, the material advantages of continued control may outweigh any incentive to implement the agreement.

Donors providing humanitarian aid may end up paying to keep civilians alive while decisive political control remains elsewhere. Each emergency would then produce another funding appeal, while the authority to lift the restrictions causing the emergency would remain in place. Humanitarian funding could consequently help sustain that arrangement. The proposed International Stabilization Force, tasked with demilitarization and civilian protection, would need the authority and backing to restrain abuses by all parties, including Israel.

Ceasefires Without Endings

Lebanon offers a warning. After the April truce in the Iran war, Pakistan’s prime minister said the ceasefire included Lebanon. U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Washington had agreed to no such thing. Israeli attacks in Lebanon continued while the parties disputed what the agreement covered. Lebanese civilians were exposed to violence while governments argued over whether their country was protected at all. Whoever defines a ceasefire’s scope decides whose security it guarantees.

Gaza already displays the features of a zombie conflict, with an announced ceasefire, recurring military operations, and unresolved struggles over territory and power. The danger is that this condition becomes entrenched. Diplomats go on describing a transition, while people live under a system of control that survives one round of negotiations after another.

Read our complete coverage

Israel’s War on Gaza

These conditions, though, are sustained by identifiable governments and institutions, through decisions they could make differently.

In a July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice stated that the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination could not be made conditional by the occupying power, and it concluded that Israel must end its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory as rapidly as possible. The Security Council’s Resolution 2803 places Palestinian statehood after reform and redevelopment, saying that the conditions for a credible pathway “may finally be in place” at that time. The political framework thus makes progress toward exercising an existing right dependent on conditions assessed by outside actors, while establishing their immediate authority much more clearly.

Every grant of outside authority under the ceasefire needs an expiration date: thresholds that can actually be met, independent assessors to judge them, and consequences for any party that blocks the next step. Without them, Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian self-government in Gaza will remain promises that outside actors renew indefinitely and never keep. For the families still displaced, another anniversary will mean another year in a tent or a ruined home, waiting for decisions they cannot make. Their ability to return, rebuild, and determine their own future remains subject to a political framework in which authority rests largely elsewhere. The Gaza ceasefire risks giving the structures of control that preceded the war a new institutional form, backed by the U.N. Security Council and administered indefinitely in the name of peace.

articleBody:
rune bosse’s lung trees imagine a forest on life support

Danish artist Rune Bosse places living trees on artificial life support in Lung Trees, an installation presented at the Danish Architecture Center in Copenhagen as part of its Age of Nature exhibition, which ran through September 2026. Each tree stands inside a transparent, inflated plastic enclosure, and is surrounded by mechanical equipment and artificial lighting. With their branches reaching toward overhead lamps, each tree seems to have been removed from the forest and placed under intensive care.

The installation imagines a future in which trees might depend on technology to survive, even as humans continue to depend on the ecological systems that trees help sustain. It reverses a relationship we tend to take for granted. Forests have long been described as the lungs of the planet, absorbing carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and releasing oxygen. Here, Bosse gives those lungs a mechanical counterpart, and suggests a world in which the natural systems supporting human life might themselves require artificial support.

Lungetræ / Lungenbaum, Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin, 2025. image © Victoria Tomaschko

transparent chambers breathe around living trees

The installation brings together living vegetation and an exposed network of machines. Transparent plastic sheeting stretches over metal frames, enclosing the trees while allowing visitors to see the soil and branches inside. Artificial lights illuminate the foliage, while equipment supplies air to the enclosed environment. The temporary structures have the practical appearance of makeshift greenhouses, although their association with medical equipment gives them a more unsettling character.

In a related 2025 presentation at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, titled Lungetræ / Lungenbaum, Bosse made the breathing movement particularly visible. A living tree and a section of forest floor were enclosed within a flexible PVC membrane attached to a metal framework. At regular intervals, a respirator pushed air into the structure, causing the plastic to expand and slowly collapse around the tree. The movement resembles the inflation of a giant lung, giving physical form to the invisible exchange of gases between a tree and its surroundings.

Lungetræ / Lungenbaum, Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin, 2025. image © Victoria Tomaschko

making art with living forests

Bosse’s interest in trees extends well beyond the gallery. Alongside his training at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, the artist studied forestry and nature management, developing a practice that follows the growth of living plants over time. At Oremandsgaard, an estate in southern Denmark, he has established an outdoor forest laboratory where he experiments with shaping trees as they grow. Some are bent into unusual forms, while others are guided to grow together. Their final shapes emerge over years, influenced by the conditions of the surrounding landscape.

This work grew partly from his frustration with bringing natural materials into museums, where plants often have to be cut, dried or preserved before they can be exhibited. His outdoor experiments allow trees to remain alive and continue changing long after the artist’s initial intervention. Lung Trees approaches the same relationship from a different direction. Inside the gallery, keeping the trees alive becomes part of the artwork itself, exposing the equipment and artificial conditions that make their temporary existence possible.

Træfald, HEART Museum, Herning, Denmark, 2022 | image © David Stjernholm, Rune Bosse

who keeps whom alive?

The installation touches on an uncomfortable contradiction in the way humans approach ecological preservation. By enclosing the trees and supplying them with artificial conditions, Bosse creates an image of protection that also suggests dependency. The machinery appears to care for the living organisms, yet the entire arrangement places their survival within a system designed and operated by humans. The trees remain living participants in the work, although their relationship with the surrounding environment has been fundamentally altered.

Bosse first developed Lungetræer in 2019, and its more recent presentations give the work a continuing relevance amid growing concerns about biodiversity loss and the deterioration of ecosystems. The installation offers a speculative glimpse of what technological preservation might look like when ecological conditions can no longer support life on their own. Its most unsettling quality comes from the simplicity of the scene.

A living tree stands inside a plastic chamber while a machine pushes air around it. The visitor watches the artificial lung expand and contract, confronted with the possibility that the relationship between humans and forests could one day become this fragile.

Træfald, HEART Museum, Herning, Denmark, 2022 | image © David Stjernholm, Rune Bosse

Træfald, HEART Museum, Herning, Denmark, 2022 | image © David Stjernholm, Rune Bosse

title: Radar-Armband macht den Unterarm zum Touchpad
subtitle: Auf dem kleinen Display einer Smartwatch sind komplexe Berührungsbefehle mühsam.
feedText: Ein neues Radar-Armband verlagert die Eingabe auf die Haut des Unterarms und erkennt dort auch Gesten mit zwei Fingern sowie unterschiedlich kräftigen Druck. Auf der begrenzten Bildschirmfläche von Smartwatches lässt sich zwar eine Vielzahl von Funktionen aufrufen, doch die Bedienung stößt schnell an Grenzen. articleBody:
Auf dem kleinen Display einer Smartwatch sind komplexe Berührungsbefehle mühsam. Ein neues Radar-Armband verlagert die Eingabe auf die Haut des Unterarms und erkennt dort auch Gesten mit zwei Fingern sowie unterschiedlich kräftigen Druck. Nach einer individuellen Kalibrierung erkannte der Prototyp im Versuch 92,8 Prozent der Gesten richtig.

Raleigh (U.S.A.). Auf der begrenzten Bildschirmfläche von Smartwatches lässt sich zwar eine Vielzahl von Funktionen aufrufen, doch die Bedienung stößt schnell an Grenzen. Beim Antippen kleiner Symbole verdeckt der Finger einen großen Teil des Displays, und für Mehrfinger-Gesten wie das Vergrößern einer Karte fehlt oft der Platz.

Als zusätzliche Eingabefläche bietet sich deshalb die Haut an. Zwar gab es schon Ansätze zur Gerätesteuerung über die Haut, doch dafür waren beispielsweise aufgeklebte Sensoren nötig oder es ließen sich nur einfachere Berührungen und Bewegungen erkennen.

Radar erfasst Berührungen und Fingerdruck

Forscher der North Carolina State University (NC State) um Dr. Chenhan Xu haben mit EpiPad nun ein System entwickelt, das den Unterarm neben der Smartwatch als Touchpad nutzt. Der zugehörige Radarsensor besteht aus einer rund fünf mal vier Millimeter großen Anordnung und sitzt in einem Armband am Handgelenk.

Das Gerät sendet Millimeterwellen aus und wertet ihre Reflexionen an Hand und Haut aus. Kleinste Verformungen der Haut verändern dabei die Phase der zurückkehrenden Signale, aus der spezielle Verfahren zusammen mit trainierten KI-Modellen Berührungsorte, Fingergesten und die Unterscheidung zwischen leichtem und kräftigem Drücken ableiten.

„Unser Ziel war es, eine kleine, tragbare Technologie zu entwickeln, die Nutzern dieses Maß an interaktiver Steuerung ermöglicht“, erklärt Dr. Chenhan Xu.

Die nutzbare Fläche erstreckt sich über etwa 15 mal vier Zentimeter des Unterarms und ist damit deutlich größer als ein Uhrendisplay. Darauf lassen sich mit einem oder zwei Fingern unter anderem Schieben, Antippen, Drehen und Zoomen als Steuerbefehle ausführen.

Gesten nach kurzem Anlernen zuverlässig erkannt

Für die Prüfung des Prototyps absolvierten 20 Personen im Alter zwischen 22 und 35 Jahren verschiedene Eingaben. Ohne Anpassung an neue Nutzer erreichte die Gestenerkennung zunächst nur 56,7 Prozent Genauigkeit. Nach einer einmaligen Kalibrierung von drei Minuten und 54 Sekunden stieg dieser Wert auf 92,8 Prozent.

Leichten und kräftigen Fingerdruck unterschied EpiPad nach der Kalibrierung in 90,2 Prozent der Fälle korrekt. Bei der Bestimmung der Berührungsposition betrug der mittlere Fehler 10,2 Millimeter, was die räumliche Präzision der Steuerung begrenzt.

In einer weiteren Untersuchung mit zwölf Teilnehmern verglich das Team die Bedienung kleiner Bildschirmziele über EpiPad, einen herkömmlichen Touchscreen und einen per Handgelenkneigung gesteuerten Cursor. Bei dieser konkreten Aufgabe lag die Fehlerquote mit EpiPad bei 6,5 Prozent, gegenüber 7,4 Prozent beim Neigungscursor und 21,7 Prozent beim Touchscreen. Die mittlere Bearbeitungszeit war mit 2,82 Sekunden ebenfalls etwas kürzer als bei den beiden Vergleichsverfahren.

Für den Alltag sind weitere Schritte nötig

Noch ist EpiPad kein eigenständig arbeitendes Smartwatch-System. Beim Echtzeitversuch wurden die Radardaten über ein Kabel an einen Laptop übertragen und dort ausgewertet, während ein separates kleines Display die Eingaben sichtbar machte. Der Prototyp muss zudem mit rund 14 Millimetern Abstand zur Haut montiert werden, was für dünnere Uhren eine andere Sensorkonstruktion erfordern könnte.

Nicht jede Eingabe reagiert gleich schnell. Normale Fingergesten wurden im Mittel nach 90 Millisekunden erkannt, bei der Unterscheidung der Druckstärke dauerte es wegen der nötigen Signalauswertung dagegen 470 Millisekunden. Außerdem zeigte ein kleiner Zusatzversuch mit nur zwei Personen, dass locker sitzende Kleidung die Erkennung deutlich verschlechtert.

Das Radar könnte künftig in das Gehäuse einer Smartwatch integriert werden und möglicherweise auch die Steuerung bildschirmloser Geräte wie Datenbrillen erleichtern. Die geschätzten Bauteilkosten von weniger als zehn US-Dollar sind allerdings noch kein Produktpreis. Ob sich das Verfahren im Alltag bei unterschiedlichen Bewegungen und Nutzern langfristig bewährt, muss weiter untersucht werden.

articleBody:
Jason Snell:

The hardware is solid and coherent, the screen a pleasure to touch
and tilt. In terms of software, though, the HomeView feels like a
peculiar amalgam of numerous other Apple products. Its main
interface makes it look a bit like an overgrown Apple Watch,
complete with customizable “faces” that sometimes resemble actual
Apple Watch faces and other times resemble the iPhone’s StandBy
mode. Its apps sometimes feel like they’ve escaped from the iPhone
or iPad, but at other times they feel more like they’re right off
of an Apple TV. And still other “apps” resemble what you might see
in your car, since Apple is also using CarPlay to project
interfaces from apps running on your iPhone.

Given the fact that this product’s tech stack feels like it
was created in a blender, it’s remarkable that it holds
together as well as it does — but there are still places
where the seams show.

I’ve been testing a review unit HomeView for a bit over a week, but haven’t had much time to devote to it. So in a lot of ways my HomeView experience thus far has been much more like that of a casual user than an expert. I plugged it in, set it up, got my wife and son to do what they needed to do to become recognized fellow-family-member users, and then we all collectively have had a week of “Well, now what?”

What Snell writes above succinctly and sharply describes my take: the hardware is top-notch but the software is like bits of iOS, WatchOS, tvOS, and CarPlay cut up and assembled into a ransom letter. The software lacks cohesion and vision and polish. If you open a web page you can select text, with the iOS touch interface, but there is nothing you can do with a text selection. You can’t copy it or share it. So why can you even make a selection? That’s the least of HomeView’s software problems, but perhaps most emblematic of its “created in a blender” state.

★

articleBody:
Field-Recordings und selbst aufgenommene Samples sind einer der einfachsten Wege zu individuellen Sounds. Pünktlich zur Adventszeit zeigen Focusrite und Novation, wie man Beats aus „gefundenen“ Geräuschen baut.

Beats aus gefundenen Geräuschen

Deine Sample-Library wird dir zu langweilig und am Ende klingt alles immer irgendwie gleich? Du bist auf der Suche nach neuen Inspirationsquellen für deine Tracks? Dann ist es höchste Zeit, rauszugehen und die Welt um dich herum aufzunehmen! Denn nichts klingt so einzigartig wie Beats aus gefundenen Geräuschen.

Optimal ausgerüstet bist du zum Beispiel mit einem kleinen Sampler wie dem Roland P-6*, der in die Jackentasche passt und ein eingebautes Mikrofon hat. Dank des integrierten Sequencers kannst du dann sogar gleich loslegen mit dem Beatmaking. Oder du legst dir einen kleinen Field-Recorder wie den Zoom M2 MicTrak* zu – gerade in den Cyber Deals im Angebot mit 30 % Rabatt!

articleBody:
Grausame Opferrituale, friedlicher Alltag: An Perus Nordküste fanden sich bei Ausgrabungen zahlreiche Hinweise auf Menschenopfer. Doch eine neue Untersuchung offenbart auffällig wenige Knochenverletzungen durch zwischenmenschliche Gewalt. Über mehr als 3.000 Jahre hinweg ließ sich zudem kein klarer Zusammenhang zwischen solchen Verletzungen und starken El-Niño-Fluten oder veränderten Niederschlägen erkennen.

Die Schädelverletzung deutet wahrscheinlich auf zwischenmenschliche Gewalt hin, der Knochenschaden eher auf einen Unfall © Snyder & Klaus, Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology

New York (U.S.A.). An der Nordküste Perus konnten extreme Klimaschwankungen das Leben ganzer Gesellschaften erschüttern. Bei El-Niño-Ereignissen ließen heftige Regenfälle die sonst trockenen Täler überfluten, während Veränderungen im Meer die Fischerei beeinträchtigten. Archäologische Fundstätten zeugen außerdem von Menschenopfern, die teilweise mit Umweltkatastrophen in Verbindung gebracht werden.

Doch was bedeuten diese außergewöhnlichen Rituale für das Leben jenseits der Tempel? Ob Umweltstress auch gewaltsame Auseinandersetzungen zwischen Menschen häufiger machte, war bislang kaum systematisch untersucht. Aufschluss können Verletzungen an Schädelknochen geben, die auf Konflikte hindeuten, sowie Schäden an anderen Knochen, die eher von Unfällen stammen können.

25 Gewalthinweise unter 1.519 Skeletten

Forscher der New York University (NYU) um Dr. Thomas J. Snyder haben nun Skelettdaten von 30 Fundorten im Lambayeque-Tal ausgewertet. Der untersuchte Zeitraum umfasst mehr als 3.000 Jahre und reicht bis in die spanische Kolonialzeit. Von zunächst 1.659 dokumentierten Menschen blieben 1.633 nach dem Ausschluss ungenau datierter Fälle in der zeitlichen Analyse.

Bei 1.519 Menschen waren die Knochen gut genug erhalten, um nach Verletzungsspuren zu suchen. Nur 25 von ihnen, entsprechend 1,6 Prozent, trugen Schädelverletzungen, die zu zwischenmenschlicher Gewalt passen. Bei 77 Menschen, rund 5,1 Prozent, fanden sich andere Knochenverletzungen, die eher auf Unfälle hindeuten.

„Am meisten überraschte uns, wie wenige Fälle zwischenmenschlicher Gewalt wir außerhalb ritualisierter Zusammenhänge beobachteten“, erklärt Dr. Thomas J. Snyder.

Kein erkennbarer Anstieg bei El Niño

Um mögliche Klimaeinflüsse zu prüfen, verglich das Team die Verletzungsmuster mit rekonstruierten Niederschlägen im Hochland und der geschätzten Häufigkeit von El-Niño-Überflutungen. Die Umweltinformationen stammen aus Klimamodellen und Rekonstruktionen, nicht aus direkten Messungen jener Zeit. Die statistische Auswertung berücksichtigte außerdem unter anderem Alter, Geschlecht und Fundorte.

Das Ergebnis: Weder häufigere El-Niño-Fluten noch veränderte Hochlandniederschläge zeigten einen klaren statistischen Zusammenhang mit den beiden Arten von Knochenverletzungen. Auch bei mutmaßlichen Gewaltverletzungen ließ sich kein deutlicher Unterschied zwischen Männern und Frauen feststellen. Hinweise auf Unfallverletzungen waren hingegen bei älteren Menschen und möglicherweise auch bei Männern häufiger.

Opferrituale waren nicht der Alltag

Auf den ersten Blick scheint dieser Befund kaum zu den grausamen Menschenopfern an Perus Nordküste zu passen. Aus dem Umfeld der Moche- und Sicán-Kulturen sind umfangreiche Opferrituale bekannt, die mit politischen Krisen und extremen Wetterereignissen in Verbindung stehen. Daraus lässt sich jedoch nicht ableiten, dass Gewalt im alltäglichen Zusammenleben ähnlich verbreitet war.

Auch die zeitliche Nähe zwischen einzelnen Opferstätten und El Niño beweist keine unmittelbare Auslösung der Rituale durch die Überschwemmungen. Die Menschenopfer könnten zugleich religiöse Vorstellungen und die politische Machtausübung der damaligen Eliten widerspiegeln. Rituale und nicht ritualisierte Gewalt müssen deshalb getrennt untersucht werden.

„Gewalt und gesellschaftlicher Zerfall sind niemals zwangsläufig“, erklärt Prof. Haagen D. Klaus von der George Mason University.

Warum der Befund keinen völligen Frieden beweist

Eine mögliche Erklärung für die wenigen Gewalthinweise ist die Vielfalt der Ressourcen an der Küste. Fischerei, verschiedene Lebensräume und Handelsbeziehungen könnten Engpässe bei Ernten teilweise abgefedert haben. Wie stark diese Möglichkeiten tatsächlich vor Konflikten schützten, wurde in der Studie allerdings nicht direkt getestet.

Zudem verraten Knochen nur einen Ausschnitt der Gewaltgeschichte. Viele Übergriffe hinterlassen keine Spuren am Skelett, und die Zahl der erkannten Schädelverletzungen ist für statistische Vergleiche klein. Weil zahlreiche Bestattungen nur näherungsweise datiert sind, könnten kurze Phasen erhöhter Gewalt zudem verborgen geblieben sein. Auch politische Unterdrückung und andere Formen struktureller Gewalt werden durch die Knochenbefunde nicht erfasst.

Trotz dieser Grenzen spricht die Untersuchung gegen eine einfache Gleichung von Klimastress und zunehmender Alltagsgewalt. Extreme Umweltveränderungen müssen gesellschaftliches Zusammenleben nicht zwangsläufig gewalttätiger machen. Welche Rolle Ressourcen, soziale Regeln und politische Entscheidungen dabei jeweils spielten, bleibt allerdings offen.

„Das unterstreicht, dass verbreitete Gewalt keine zwangsläufige Reaktion auf den Klimawandel ist. Als Gesellschaft können und müssen wir entscheiden, wie wir mit unserer eigenen Klimakrise umgehen“, betont Dr. Thomas J. Snyder.

title: Loyalty Blocks Accountability

feedText:

articleBody:
We moderns tell ourselves that while the ancients were transparently and strongly dominated by elites, we hold our leaders far more accountable, such as via law, media, and democracy. But we allow our elites many easy ways to use money or political connections to gain far more favorable treatment from media and law. And we use democracy much more to fight each other via coalition politics than to hold leaders accountable. That is, we much more submit to the leaders we vote for, than we defy the leaders we don’t.

Consider 18 ways we now block holding our leaders accountable:

We make blackmail illegal, so they are less penalized for misbehavior.

We don’t arrange to try to secretly and randomly bribe officials.

We don’t expect leaders to post bonds they forfeit if not keep promises.

We mostly pick leaders on recommendation of other leaders.

We rarely collect track records re their performance outcomes, or predictions.

We rarely use prediction/decision markets to check leader prediction/decisions.

We let firms pick their own auditors, and audits are rarely randomized.

Evaluators usually can’t see leader decision internal records.

Old leaders are not given regular tests re dementia.

We don’t much protect or reward whistleblowers.

Leader evaluations are rarely blinded.

360 reviews are rare and toothless.

Only for-profit leaders have much cash performance incentives.

We give police, prosecutors, and govt officials have legal immunity.

Police internal affairs reports to police chief, not mayor.

Firms use poison pills to block takeovers, and we vilify short sellers.

Golden parachutes and option price resetting cushion CEO losses.

We let CEOs pick who is on their boards.

Many excuses are offered for each of these patterns, but the obvious explanation here is that we are far more like the ancients than we like to think. We are eager to submit to the powerful, and show them our fealty, and are wary of endorsing positions by which we might seem to challenge or defy their power.

This is a big problem with two of my solutions to cultural drift, which require at least some of our groups to adopt much more competent forms of governance, forms that induce leaders to actually achieve identified goals. Our world now far less achieves most of the goals we give our leaders, due to our using pretty bad governance mechanisms. But we each prefer that to risking our seeming less loyal to our elites.

title: Erdkruste ist wohl schon vor 3,95 Milliarden Jahren tief abgesunken
subtitle: Aus der Frühzeit der Erde sind kaum Gesteine erhalten, die ihre ursprüngliche Entstehungsgeschichte bewahrt haben.
feedText:

articleBody:
Aus der Frühzeit der Erde sind kaum Gesteine erhalten, die ihre ursprüngliche Entstehungsgeschichte bewahrt haben. Ein 3,95 Milliarden Jahre alter Gneis aus Nordchina enthält nun chemische Spuren von Kruste, die zunächst nahe der Oberfläche verändert und anschließend tief versenkt wurde. Dies könnte auf eine frühe, zeitweise Form der Subduktion hindeuten.

Feldaufnahmen und Mikroskopbilder des 3,95 Milliarden Jahre alten Trondhjemit-Gneises © Nature

Peking (China). Wann begann die Erdkruste, sich in bewegliche Platten zu gliedern und an ihren Rändern in den Erdmantel abzutauchen? Diese Frage gehört zu den großen Rätseln der Erdgeschichte, weil fast alle Gesteine aus der ersten halben Milliarde Jahre unseres Planeten längst umgewandelt oder zerstört sind. Mit ihnen verschwanden auch viele Spuren der ersten Krustenbewegungen.

Einige wenige Gesteinsreste geben dennoch Einblick in diese Ära. Zu ihnen zählt der mehr als vier Milliarden Jahre alte Acasta-Gneis aus Kanada, dessen Entstehung überwiegend auf vergleichsweise geringe Tiefen hindeutet. Andere Untersuchungen lieferten bereits indirekte Hinweise auf eine sehr frühe Subduktion, doch die Abläufe der damaligen Krustenbildung bleiben umstritten.

Geologische Karten des Untersuchungsgebiets © Nature

Gneis aus der Frühzeit der Erde

Forscher der Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences (CAGS) um Prof. Yusheng Wan haben nun einen ungewöhnlich alten Gneis aus dem Shimen-Komplex in der nordchinesischen Provinz Hebei untersucht. Der sogenannte Trondhjemit-Gneis ist aus einem einstigen siliziumreichen Magma hervorgegangen und wurde später durch Druck und Wärme umgeformt. Drei Proben des Gesteins lieferten die Grundlage für die Analysen.

Zur Altersbestimmung nutzte das Team winzige Zirkonkristalle im Gneis. Das Verhältnis von Uran zu dessen Zerfallsprodukt Blei ergab aus 33 geeigneten Messungen ein Kristallisationsalter von 3.951 ± 3 Millionen Jahren. Damit gehört der Fund zu den ältesten zuverlässig datierten Gesteinen der Erde und ermöglicht einen seltenen direkten Blick auf Prozesse vor knapp vier Milliarden Jahren.

Interne Zirkonstrukturen und SHRIMP-U-Pb-Daten des 3,95 Milliarden Jahre alten Trondhjemit-Gneises © Nature

Spuren von Wasser und frühem Krustenwachstum

Die Zirkone verraten zugleich etwas über die Herkunft des einstigen Magmas. Ihr ungewöhnlich hoher Anteil des schweren Sauerstoffisotops Sauerstoff-18 weist darauf hin, dass das basaltische Ausgangsgestein zuvor durch Wasser bei niedrigen Temperaturen verändert worden war. Dies könnte an oder nahe der damaligen Erdoberfläche geschehen sein.

Auch die Hafniumisotope in den Zirkonen sind aufschlussreich. Ihre Zusammensetzung deutet darauf hin, dass das Ausgangsmaterial aus einem Erdmantel stammte, dem bei früherer Schmelzbildung bereits Bestandteile für neue Erdkruste entzogen worden waren. Modellrechnungen verlegen diese Trennung von Mantel und Kruste möglicherweise auf die Zeit vor rund 4,3 Milliarden Jahren, also lange vor die Entstehung des untersuchten Gneises.

Schmelze aus mehr als 50 Kilometern Tiefe

Die chemischen Spuren deuten zudem auf eine Entstehung des Magmas unter hohem Druck hin. Thermodynamische und geochemische Modelle ergeben, dass etwa acht bis 16 Prozent einer basaltischen Ausgangskruste bei mehr als 1,6 Gigapascal und Temperaturen von 740 bis 820 Grad Celsius aufgeschmolzen sein könnten. Der Druck entspricht einer Versenkung auf mehr als 50 Kilometer Tiefe.

Besonders auffällig ist die Kombination aus großer Tiefe und vergleichsweise niedriger Temperatur. Das zuvor durch Wasser veränderte Gestein muss demnach wahrscheinlich recht schnell in die Tiefe gelangt sein, bevor es sich stärker erwärmen konnte. Als plausibelste Erklärung schlagen die Studienautoren ein zeitlich begrenztes Abtauchen von Kruste vor, wie es in Subduktionszonen geschieht.

Kein Beweis für moderne Plattentektonik

Die Befunde belegen allerdings keine weltweit etablierte Plattentektonik nach heutigem Muster. Die Versenkung und der angenommene Subduktionsmechanismus wurden aus Gesteinschemie und Modellrechnungen erschlossen, nicht unmittelbar an einer erhaltenen urzeitlichen Plattengrenze beobachtet. Möglich wäre damit zunächst ein regionaler und zeitlich begrenzter Vorgang.

Hinzu kommt, dass die Untersuchung auf drei Proben eines eng begrenzten Fundorts beruht. Die geochemische Deutung hängt außerdem davon ab, wie gut der Gneis die Zusammensetzung seiner ursprünglichen Schmelze bewahrt hat. Weitere ähnlich alte Gesteine müssen deshalb zeigen, ob solche tiefen Krustenbewegungen vor knapp vier Milliarden Jahren häufiger auftraten.

subtitle: Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.
feedText:

articleBody:
Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Gallery

Previous

Next

Gallery

Close

Site plan

Plan

Roof plan

Section

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel "part of the architecture itself", using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

"Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials," said the studio.

"In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment," it added.

"Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself."

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna's structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site's natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

"Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework," said the studio.

"Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest," it added. "The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

subtitle: Patrick McGee (author of Apple in China; my guest on The Talk Show last May), writing on X in response to Semafor’s reporting that Nvidia is “consi…

articleBody:
Patrick McGee (author of Apple in China; my guest on The Talk Show last May), writing on X in response to Semafor’s reporting that Nvidia is “considering” Johny Srouji:

Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji would be an incredible choice to
lead @nvidia — and I believe he’d accept it.

He’s hit the ceiling at Apple and won’t ever be CEO; obviously
competent; ambitious as hell; has long wanted chip designs to
dictate Apple product launches/timelines.

I wrote about this a few days ago, that my money is on Srouji having no interest in the Nvidia job. It’s true that Srouji will almost certainly never be CEO at Apple. But it’s wrong to assume that Srouji would consider CEO of Nvidia to be an upgrade from CHO at Apple. There’s no way Eddy Cue, Craig Federighi, or Greg Joswiak would leave Apple to be CEO at another company. Most of Apple’s leadership genuinely bleeds six colors. There’s a certain approach to product that drives them, motivates them, and literally only Apple does that type of work. Tim Cook surely turned down numerous CEO offers to leave Apple while he served as COO under Steve Jobs, and he’s always been clear that he hoped Jobs would stay a few steps ahead of his cancer and could remain at Apple until, well, probably around now. (Jobs would be 71.)

I’ve never met Srouji and don’t have a read on him like I do other leaders at Apple. But I do have a read on Ternus and Cook. I’ll stick with my bet from earlier in the week:

Another scenario is that Srouji meant what he said, loves his job
at Apple, and truly is John Ternus’s trusted and trustworthy
hardware lieutenant. In this case, Nvidia’s board leaking that
they’re considering Srouji to replace Huang is like someone in
hell saying they’re considering ordering some ice water.

Aside from Srouji’s loyalty to Apple (and to the Apple Silicon chip architecture that’s been his life’s work), there’s also the question of whether he’d take the gig at Nvidia in particular, even if he is open to leaving Apple. Jensen Huang has left the company with a $4 trillion market cap, yes, but it was $5 trillion just a week ago. It now seems 20 percent of Nvidia’s sales in the AI era have been in violation of U.S. national security export controls to China. The company has no internal leadership hierarchy. And Huang placed bets that have leveraged the company’s future on OpenAI and the overall data center mania not being a bubble. Srouji has been a senior leader at the one tech company that conspicuously avoided those bets entirely.

articleBody:
Für Stimmen und Gitarren ist der 1073 seit über 50 Jahren DIE Instanz. Bass und Snare lieben ihn aber auch. Mit USB, ADAT und cleveren neuen Monitor-Features macht AMS Neve aus dem 1073DPX-D so was wie den Volks-Neve. Ein 19-Zoll-Klotz mit Rack-Ohren und „dem“ Sound. Für alle, denen zwei gute Kanäle wichtiger sind als Immersive-Nonsens. Made in UK, Mate!

AMS Neve 1073DPX-D: Dual 1073 Channel Strip & USB/ADAT Audio Interface

Highlights AMS Neve 1073DPX-D Test: 19-Zoll-Klassiker, mit USB-2.

1073 Dual Preamps mit EQ (DPX) sowie digitalen USB und ADAT Anschlüssen (-D)

Extrem musikalischer Drei-Band-EQ, Marinair-Übertrager

Umfangreiches Monitoring, Routing für Kopfhörer und Speaker

DETAILS

Zweimal 1073, digital verpackt

AMS Neve steckt endlich ein class-compliant USB-2-Interface in den dicken Dual-Mono-Klassiker! Britische Class-A-Technik und Marinair-Übertrager treffen auf zwei Aufnahme- und vier Wiedergabekanäle per USB.

#fnet-affiliate-block-1.fnet-affiliate-block[data-show-thumbnail="false"]  Zwei Lightpipes bringen zusätzlich ADAT rein und raus, dazu gibt’s nur einen BNC-Wordclock-Ausgang. Wer den DPX-D als Zentrale nutzt, kann ein entsprechend ausgestattetes 500er-Rack oder zusätzliche ADAT-Preamps anbinden.

Bei 44,1 oder 48 kHz kommen über ADAT bis zu acht Kanäle pro Richtung dazu – genug für gelegentliche Drum-Sessions. Der DPX-D selbst arbeitet mit bis zu 24 Bit und 192 kHz. Das externe Netzteil hat einen IEC-Netzanschluss und wird per XLR mit dem Neve verbunden. Beim Rechneranschluss bleibt’s oldschool. Am Neve sitzt eine USB-B-Buchse.

Für den Kopfhörer stehen zwei Stereo-Returns aus der DAW, die Inputs und der MON/Aux-In zur Wahl. Wer mehr Cue-Mixe für die ADATs braucht, muss sie in der DAW bauen und routen oder sich ein RME Digiface besorgen. Für Dante- oder AES-Setups gibt’s andere 1073-Lösungen. Preislich spielen die dann auch in einer anderen Liga …

It’s a Classic – jetzt als Hardware-Insert

Bis zu 80 dB Gain in gerasterten Stufen, mehrere Schaltkreise, dicke Übertrager, ein musikalischer Dreiband-EQ sowie knackiger Lowcut sind die wahren Gründe, sich zwei 1073 ins Rack zu klemmen. Allein die fett- klackenden und roten Chicken-Heads…

Combos in the front, rückseitig gibt es Mic und Line auf getrennten XLRs.

Dual Preamp Equalizer Digital: DPX+D

Einen Kopfhörerausgang hatte bereits der DPX. Das Doppel „D“ in 1073DPX-D steht für Digital und mehr Monitoring – inklusive Lautstärkeregler für Main-Speaker. Selbst wenn sich die umfangreiche Bedienung nicht auf den ersten Blick erschließt, merkt man bereits nach zwei Handgriffen, dass sich die Briten Gedanken gemacht haben: wieviel Workflow man mit zwei Push-Regler mehr schaffen kann …

Alle Zusatzfunktionen lösen konkrete Aufgaben: so lässt sich die Abhörquelle für Lautsprecher und Kopfhörer getrennt schalten. Für die DAW-Wiedergabe ist der USB 1/2 den Speakern zugeordnet, über USB 3/4 lässt sich auch ein eigener Kopfhörer-Mix spielen. Der Blend-Regler mischt ferner die Direktsignale der Preamps mit der DAW-Wiedergabe.

Rechts finden sich die neuen Features für Monitoring und Co.

Über denselben Regler schaltet man die Stereoverteilung der Direktsignale: entweder ein Preamp links und der andere rechts oder eben beides mittig: MONO oder eben ST(ereo) DPX entsprechend vorn abgekürzt. Alternativ gibt es noch einen analogen MON(itor-In) auf der Rückseite, ausgestattet mit einem weiteren Stereo-XLR-In.

Außerdem führt der USB 3/4 den digitalen Rückspielweg zurück in die analogen 1073-Kanäle. So lassen sich aufgenommene Spuren nochmal durch den Neve schicken. Hardware-Insert deluxe, quasi. Einen schaltbaren, symmetrischen Analog-Insert gibt’s obendrein, mir PRE ist seine Postion im Signalfluss sogar schaltbar.

O/P Level regelt den Pegel an den XLR-Ausgängen und sitzt hinter dem EQ sowie vor dem Ausgangsübertrager. Ein Druck auf den Regler schaltet die darunterliegende Pegelanzeige zwischen Preamp, EQ/Insert und Ausgang um.

Die Sends sind ferner immer aktiv, genau wie der zusätzliche Line-Out. Wer auf ein anderes Interface umsteigt, kann den DPX-D also ohne Abstriche als analogen Channelstrip weiterverwenden. Auch wer kein USB braucht sondern nur etwas Kopfhörer-Frontend für den Musiker findet hier eine bessere Alternative als in dem 1073DPX. Das gibt Pluspunkte!

Soweit alles bei alten

Links davon ist alles wie bei den “alten Channels”. Nur die eben besprochenen Regler rechts rufen nach kurzem oder langem Druck unterschiedliche Zusatzfunktionen auf. Auf den ersten Blick wirkt das verschachtelt, geht nach paar Handgriffen aber gut in Fleisch und Blut. Alle Bedienelemente sind rustikal und großzügig dimensioniert. Die Buchsen sind alle verschraubt. Das mitgelieferte Netzteil hat jetzt sogar einen einrastenden XLR-Stecker.

Der 1073 EQ ist sehr musikalisch und flink bedient.

Umschalten statt umstecken

Pro Mono-Kanal gibt es hinten zwei XLR-Eingänge. Separat, einmal für Mikrofon und einmal Line und mit Verriegelung. Vorn nimmt eine weitere Combo-Buchse alternative Mikrofon-, Line- und Instrumentensignale an. So kann das Booth-Studiomikro fest verkabelt bleiben, während ein Synth am Line-Eingang hängt und vorn Platz für spontane DI-Action ist.

Aufgenommen werden hier aber maximal zwei Kanäle gleichzeitig – oder auch einmal Mono mit zwei Settings, wenn man kreativ ist Welche Quelle letztlich auf welchem Kanal landet, entscheidet man mit den ziemlich fetten Konsolen-Tastern vorn. Absolut souverän.

Solide verschraubte Buchsen, das sieht man gerne.

Alle anderen Standards sind selbstverständlich auch dabei. 48 Volt, ein massives −20-dB-Pad, Low-Z und DI sind an Bord. Gerade bei Low-Z und DI hätte ich mir eine etwas konsequentere Einbindung in die Quellenwahl gewünscht. Also nur von der Positionierung der Schalter her. Das wäre noch übersichtlicher – vielleicht auch endlich mit Status-LEDs. Ebenfalls auffällig ist, dass es hier nun keine verschraubten Blenden mehr gibt, um eventuell weitere Optionen nachzurüsten.

articleBody:
Wer professionell Bilder bearbeitet, kommt an Photoshop nach wie vor kaum vorbei, auch wenn günstigere Alternativen längst aufgeholt haben. Zur Hausmesse MAX legt Adobe nun mit Version 28 nach und erweitert das Programm um mehrere Werkzeuge. Die eigentlich weitreichendere Nachricht betrifft allerdings erst das kommende Jahr.

Nachträgliche Beleuchtung und ein direkter Vorher-Nachher-Vergleich

Im Zentrum des Updates steht Relight. Die Funktion erlaubt es, bis zu drei zusätzliche Lichtquellen in einem Bild zu platzieren und deren Position, Farbe, Helligkeit und Streuung unmittelbar auf der Arbeitsfläche zu verändern. Das Ausgangsmaterial bleibt dabei unangetastet, sodass sich die Lichtstimmung auch später noch korrigieren lässt. Abgerechnet wird über generative Credits: 30 Stück kostet eine Anwendung, fällig allerdings erst mit dem Klick auf „Fertig“ – das Experimentieren in der Vorschau ist kostenfrei. Ganz ohne künstliche Intelligenz kommt Quick Compare aus. Bearbeitungen lassen sich damit wahlweise in einer geteilten Ansicht oder durch Umschalten mit dem Original vergleichen – ein Prinzip, das Lightroom-Nutzern bereits vertraut sein dürfte.

Gründlichere Retusche und flexible Bildformate

Überarbeitet hat Adobe außerdem das Entfernen-Werkzeug. Es soll nun erkennen, was zu einem Objekt gehört, und Schatten, Spiegelungen sowie laut Hersteller sogar Fußspuren oder Wellen gleich mit beseitigen. Bislang war an dieser Stelle häufig Nacharbeit von Hand nötig.

Eingebetteten Inhalt von YouTube öffnen

Ergänzend dazu passt Generative Recompose Bildinhalte an veränderte Formate an, indem Motive neu positioniert und fehlende Hintergrundbereiche aufgefüllt werden. Adobe selbst führt die Funktion vorerst noch unter den Beta-Neuerungen. Ebenfalls an Bord sind die Bearbeitung per Texteingabe, deren Ergebnisse sich anschließend weiter verfeinern lassen, sowie eine KI-gestützte Hochskalierung, die neben der Auflösung auch den Detailgrad erhöhen soll.

Creative Cloud wird zur Schnittstelle für KI-Agenten

Über Photoshop hinaus weist eine Ankündigung, die Adobe am Rande platziert hat: Ab Anfang 2027 sollen die Creative-Cloud-Programme das Model Context Protocol (MCP) unterstützen. Dabei handelt es sich um einen offenen Standard, über den KI-Systeme auf Funktionen anderer Anwendungen zugreifen. Vorgesehen ist die Anbindung für Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere und After Effects, zunächst im Rahmen einer geschlossenen Beta.

Als Anwendungsfall nennt der Softwarekonzern etwa den Auftrag, ein Logo aus sämtlichen Motiven einer Kampagne zu entfernen, ohne jede Datei einzeln öffnen zu müssen. Die Verbindung läuft lokal auf dem Rechner, die Projektdateien bleiben mitsamt ihren Ebenen vollständig bearbeitbar. Im Zusammenspiel mit weiteren Diensten werden auch längere Abläufe denkbar, bei denen ein Assistent Vorgaben aus einem Dokument übernimmt, die Änderungen ausführt und das Ergebnis über Slack bereitstellt.

Adobe setzt damit den Kurs fort, klassische Werkzeuge und KI-Funktionen enger zu verzahnen, Apfelpage berichtete. Photoshop 28 lässt sich ab sofort über die Creative-Cloud-App installieren. Ob sich die MCP-Öffnung im Produktionsalltag als echte Entlastung erweist oder vor allem auf der Bühne gut aussieht, wird sich erst zeigen, wenn die Schnittstelle tatsächlich verfügbar ist.
