articleBody:
Steinzeitlicher Trinkgenuss: Bereits vor rund 5.000 Jahren dürften Menschen im Osten Chinas vergorene Reisgetränke durch Gewebe gefiltert haben. Darauf deuten Rückstände von Reis, Schimmelpilzen und feinen Pflanzenfasern an speziellen Tongefäßen hin. Die Funde machen eine bislang nur vermutete Funktion dieser Keramik greifbar und geben Einblick in die mögliche Bedeutung des Alkohols für damalige Bestattungsrituale.

Die schematische Rekonstruktion zeigt die Herstellung und den Verzehr von Lebensmitteln an der Fundstätte Wayaoli © Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences

Tucson (U.S.A.). Alkoholische Getränke wurden in mehreren Teilen der Welt schon in vorgeschichtlicher Zeit hergestellt. Doch welche Geräte die Menschen beim Brauen nutzten, lässt sich oft nur schwer aus archäologischen Funden ablesen.

Ein besonderer Keramiktyp aus der Region am unteren Jangtse war deshalb lange ein Rätsel. Bei diesen Gefäßen sind eine obere und eine untere Schale so verbunden, dass Flüssigkeit zwischen ihnen ablaufen kann. Ob sie tatsächlich zum Filtern von Reiswein oder für andere Arbeitsschritte bei der Lebensmittelverarbeitung dienten, war jedoch offen.

Reis und roter Schimmel im Tongefäß

Forscher der University of Arizona (UArizona) um Dr. Ran Chen haben nun 16 Keramikgefäße aus Wayaoli in der chinesischen Provinz Zhejiang untersucht. Die etwa 5.300 bis 5.000 Jahre alten Fundstücke umfassen fünf mutmaßliche Filter sowie Kochgefäße, Vorratsbehälter und Teller zum Vergleich.

Unter dem Mikroskop suchte das Team nach Stärkekörnchen, pflanzlichen Kieselpartikeln, Pilzresten und winzigen Fasern. An allen fünf Filtern fanden sich Reisrückstände und Spuren von Monascus-Schimmelpilzen, die bei traditionellen Verfahren zur Herstellung vergorener Reisgetränke eingesetzt werden. Einige veränderte Stärkekörnchen weisen zudem auf Erhitzen und Fermentation hin.

Die Pilze können Stärke mithilfe von Enzymen in vergärbaren Zucker umwandeln und bilden rote Farbstoffe. Deshalb könnte das damalige Getränk eine rötliche Farbe besessen haben. Neben Reis zeigen die Rückstände weitere stärkehaltige Pflanzen, darunter die Samen einer Wasserpflanze und Hiobstränen, doch die genaue Rezeptur lässt sich daraus nicht rekonstruieren.

Feine Fasern statt grober Sieböffnungen

Besonders aufschlussreich sind mikroskopische Pflanzenfasern, die an vier der fünf Filter sowie an zwei weiteren Keramikfragmenten nachgewiesen wurden. Überwiegend handelte es sich um Bastfasern, also Fasern aus dem inneren Rindengewebe von Pflanzenstängeln, die sich zu Stoff verarbeiten lassen.

An den untersuchten Koch- und Vorratsgefäßen sowie Tellern fehlten entsprechende Faserreste dagegen. Zusammen mit der besonderen Gefäßform spricht diese Verteilung dafür, dass ein Gewebe die oberen Schalen auskleidete. Es könnte feine Rückstände des vergorenen Reises zurückgehalten haben, während die Flüssigkeit in den unteren Teil ablief.

Allerdings ist kein Stück des vermuteten Textils erhalten geblieben. Auch die Pflanzenart, aus der das Gewebe bestanden haben könnte, ließ sich nicht bestimmen. Die Stoffeinlage ist daher eine Rekonstruktion aus mikroskopischen Spuren und Gefäßbauweise, kein direkt erhaltener Fund.

Mehr als ein Getränk für den Alltag

Die keramischen Filter stammen auch aus Gräbern, in denen sie gemeinsam mit anderem Haushaltsgeschirr niedergelegt wurden. Ihre wiederholte Verwendung als Grabbeigaben deutet darauf hin, dass die Herstellung und der Genuss vergorener Reisgetränke im gesellschaftlichen und rituellen Leben eine Rolle spielten.

Die Herstellung solcher Getränke war in der Region allerdings noch deutlich älter. Bereits an der etwa 10.000 bis 9.000 Jahre alten Fundstätte Shangshan wurden Hinweise auf Reisgärung mit Monascus-Pilzen entdeckt. Neu an den Funden von Wayaoli ist vor allem der Hinweis darauf, wie die Menschen später Flüssigkeit und feste Gärungsreste voneinander trennten.

Damit rückt ein weiterer Schritt der frühen Brautechnik ins Licht. Unklar bleibt allerdings, wie die Filter im Detail verwendet wurden, welche Textilien zum Einsatz kamen und wie das Getränk tatsächlich schmeckte.

Originalstudie im Fachmagazin Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), doi: 10.1073/pnas.2412274121

Die Funde machen eine bislang nur vermutete Funktion dieser Keramik greifbar und geben Einblick in die mögliche Bedeutung des Alkohols für damalige Bestattungsrituale. articleBody:
iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max und iPhone Duo sind bereits „abgearbeitet“. Mit den nächsten neuen iPhone-Modellen wird im Frühjahr 2027 gerechnet. Dann sollen ebenfalls drei neue Modelle angekündigt werden und auf den Markt kommen. Die Rede ist vom iPhone 18, iPhone 18e und iPhone Air 2.

Fotocredit: Apple

iPhone 18 und iPhone 18e sollen im Frühjahr 2027 mit A20 Chip erscheinen

Apple wird das iPhone 18 und das günstigere iPhone 18e voraussichtlich im Frühjahr 2027 vorstellen. Das hat Bloomberg-Journalist Mark Gurman in der aktuellen Folge seines Newsletters beziehungsweise Podcasts „Power On“ erneut bestätigt. Es heißt, dass beide Modelle mit Apples neuem A20-Chip ausgerüstet werden.

Damit setzt Apple offenbar seine neue Strategie eines geteilten iPhone-Produktstarts fort. Während das iPhone 18 Pro, das iPhone 18 Pro Max und das erste faltbare iPhone Duo bereits im Herbst 2026 mit dem A20 Pro erschienen sind, verschiebt der Konzern die günstigeren Modelle ins nächste Frühjahr. Dann soll auch der A20 Chip debütieren.

Neben dem iPhone 18 und dem iPhone 18e soll im selben Zeitraum auch das iPhone Air 2 auf den Markt kommen.

Der A20-Chip wird voraussichtlich im moderneren 2-Nanometer-Verfahren gefertigt. Für das iPhone 18 und das iPhone 18e werden zudem neun Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher erwartet. Das wäre ein Gigabyte mehr als bei den entsprechenden Vorgängermodellen und könnte insbesondere anspruchsvollere Apple-Intelligence-Funktionen unterstützen.

Als möglicher Zeitraum für die Vorstellung gelten März oder April 2027. Mit dem gestaffelten Veröffentlichungsplan verteilt Apple seine iPhone-Neuheiten erstmals deutlich stärker über das Jahr.

title: Archivist Discovers Rare Photo of Abraham Lincoln at Gettysburg Nearly a Century Later
subtitle: Portrait of Abraham Lincoln.
feedText:
(Photo: PHOTOGRAPHER/AUTHOR'S NAME via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain)

articleBody:
Portrait of Abraham Lincoln. (Photo: PHOTOGRAPHER/AUTHOR'S NAME via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain)

For nearly 90 years, a damaged glass plate negative concealed a remarkable piece of American history. Cataloged as a crowd scene, the photograph showed spectators gathered around a platform in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. In 1952, archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged the image and discovered Abraham Lincoln standing among the crowd. The photograph captured the president at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery on November 19, 1863, the same day he delivered the Gettysburg Address.

Cobb joined the U.S. National Archives in 1936. Her work focused on historical photographs, including Civil War images. When she examined the glass plate, she suspected it might depict the Gettysburg ceremony. A tall flag helped her locate the speakers’ platform. She then enlarged that section to examine the figures more closely.

The result revealed a small, bare-headed man with a beard and a distinctive profile. Cobb identified him as Lincoln. She also recognized Ward Hill Lamon, the president’s bodyguard and the ceremony’s chief marshal, along with Pennsylvania Governor Andrew Curtin. Other figures have been proposed as members of Lincoln’s party, though some identifications remain disputed.

The photograph belonged to a collection associated with Civil War photographer Mathew Brady. The U.S. government purchased Brady’s photographic collection in the 1870s, and the material eventually entered the National Archives. However, the photographer who took this particular image remains unknown. The glass plate had also lost roughly a quarter of its upper-left corner, further complicating its examination.

Cobb estimated that the photograph was taken around noon, when Lincoln arrived at the platform. His famous address came approximately three hours later. The image does not capture the speech itself. Instead, it offers a rare glimpse of Lincoln at the ceremony before he delivered one of the most enduring speeches in American history.

The discovery became public on February 12, 1953, Lincoln’s birthday. The Gettysburg Times reported the finding, and Life magazine later published the image. Early coverage approached the identification cautiously because the figure’s face was blurred. Lincoln occupies only a small portion of the original photograph, making historical context essential to the identification.

Cobb’s discovery reflected years of experience examining archival images. Her work illustrates why historical photographs deserve more than a cursory glance. A vague catalog entry had obscured the significance of the Gettysburg image for decades. By questioning its description and carefully examining the evidence, Cobb brought a long-overlooked piece of history into view.

In 1952, National Archives archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged a damaged glass plate negative and discovered Abraham Lincoln in a crowd at Gettysburg.

A modern enlargement printed from the original glass plate, held by the Library of Congress and shown in its American Treasures exhibit. Lincoln is the hatless, bearded figure just left of center; the Library lists John Hay, John Nicolay, Edward Everett and Gettysburg attorney David Wills among the surrounding figures scholars have argued over. Photographer attributions vary from unidentified to Mathew Brady to David Bachrach. (Photo: Library of Congress, Public domain)

The photograph captures Lincoln at the November 19, 1863, cemetery dedication, hours before he delivered the Gettysburg Address.

Crowd of citizens, soldiers, and etc. with Abraham Lincoln at Gettysburg. (Photo: National Archives Catalog, Public domain)

Mislabeled for nearly 90 years, the photograph was identified through Cobb’s research and careful examination of the original glass plate.

Cobb in the Still Picture stacks, holding a Brady photograph of the 20th Maine Infantry Regiment, with Brady portraits of Abraham Lincoln and Hannibal Hamlin on the shelf behind her. The Archives caption on the print calls her Archivist in Charge of the Still Picture Branch. (Photo: National Archives Catalog, Public domain)

Source: A National Archives Archivist Enlarged a Mislabeled Glass Plate in 1952 and Found Lincoln at Gettysburg

articleBody:
The Shepherd’s Dream from “Paradise Lost,” by Henry Fuseli, via WikiArt.

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at a Brooklyn building collapse, BAAJA’s odds of passing, reusing old memory in new phones, a nationwide aircraft ground stop, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

Housing and Cities

A 3 story building in New York partially collapsed into an adjacent construction site that was being excavated, killing 8 people and injuring 18. Good reminder that for as burdensome as various building regulations can sometimes be (particularly in New York, with its ubiquitous sidewalk sheds), they don’t exist for no reason. [Construction Dive]

On the other hand, that doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t evaluate code requirements to see if the benefits they bring are worth the cost. An article in the Washington Post argues that many requirements to upgrade electrical panels for higher load devices are often unnecessary. “Outdated industry practices and in some places outdated electrical codes are regularly resulting in the recommendation that people need to upgrade their electrical panels if they want to add appliances such as induction stoves, heat pumps and electric-vehicle chargers. The expense — at a median of $3,500, and triple or quadruple that in some settings — is deterring some energy-efficient upgrades and making the projects far more costly for those who proceed. But some researchers say panel upgrades are almost always unnecessary. One report this year found that 98 percent of homes with 100-ampere panels, the smallest common size, have room to add popular electronic devices.” [Washington Post]

The US now has over 1500 mass timber buildings, up from fewer than 100 a decade ago. [The Real Deal]

The current probability of permitting reform bill BAAJA becoming law is little over 50% on Kalshi. [Kalshi]

A Houthi missile hit Saudi state oil company Aramco’s skyscraper in Riyadh. [X]

A new Nicholas Bagley paper on the cost of federal permitting, arguing that the real costs of things like NEPA is the huge amount of effort agencies put in to try and make things “litigation proof”. “The evidence does suggest, however, that the bulk of the costs of the federal permitting regime stem from the defensive measures agencies and developers take to guard against the risk of a bad outcome in court. That insight allows for a rough evaluation of the likely effects of popular permitting reform ideas. Some—including popular ones like time limits and statutes of limitations—are unlikely to accomplish much. Only those reforms that change the incentives created by the risk of judicial review will meaningfully move the needle.” [Nicholas Bagley]

A progress report from the Center for Land Economics, which advocates for land value taxes to make more efficient use of urban land. ”Three states passed laws enabling land value taxes in some form: Kentucky, Virginia and New York. In each of them we’re now helping cities work out how to put them into practice. Five more states and DC considered similar bills. This is the most legislative momentum the movement has seen in decades…” [Land Economics]

articleBody:
On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.

When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms.

But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articleBody:
There are many art fairs in New York City, but perhaps none are friendlier than the one hosted by the chummy Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA).

“We all know each other very well,” Dorsey Waxter, former president of the ADAA and partner at Van Doren Waxter gallery, told Hyperallergic. “We’ve vetted each gallery that comes into the association for levels of excellence and standards. And it’s not so big you can’t have conversations with dealers and find out things about what you’re looking at.”

Jovial conversations about pathbreaking newcomers and long-dead modernists abounded inside the Park Avenue Armory, which provided a needed refuge from the cold nor’easter pummeling Manhattan for Thursday night’s VIP preview.

title: iPhone Duo im Dauertest: CNET faltet bis zum Zerbrechen
subtitle: Die spannendste Frage bei faltbaren Smartphones ist stets die Stabilität des Faltmechanismus.
feedText: Das iPhone Duo hat hier laut Apple eine der ausgereiftesten und komplexesten Konstruktionen am Markt vorzuweisen, aber wie lange hält es im Alltag wirklich durch? Die einzige Möglichkeit, außer Jahre auf erste Erfahrungsberichte zu warten, sind Dauertests in mechanischen Testszenarien. So einer läuft aktuell und er zeigt erstaunliche Resultate. Wie oft kann man das iPhone Duo öffnen und schließen, bevor es den Geist aufgibt? Apples erstes faltbares iPhone zeigt nach mehr als 450.000 Öffnungs- und Schließvorgänge…
articleBody:
Die spannendste Frage bei faltbaren Smartphones ist stets die Stabilität des Faltmechanismus.

Das iPhone Duo hat hier laut Apple eine der ausgereiftesten und komplexesten Konstruktionen am Markt vorzuweisen, aber wie lange hält es im Alltag wirklich durch?

Die einzige Möglichkeit, außer Jahre auf erste Erfahrungsberichte zu warten, sind Dauertests in mechanischen Testszenarien. So einer läuft aktuell und er zeigt erstaunliche Resultate.

Wie oft kann man das iPhone Duo öffnen und schließen, bevor es den Geist aufgibt? Apples erstes faltbares iPhone zeigt nach mehr als 450.000 Öffnungs- und Schließvorgängen erste deutliche Verschleißerscheinungen. Das US-Technikportal CNET unterzieht das iPhone Duo seit rund drei Wochen einem automatisierten Belastungstest, der per Livestream übertragen wird. Während sich das Scharnier inzwischen nicht mehr vollständig selbstständig öffnet, funktionieren Display und übrige Gerätefunktionen weiterhin.

Der Dauertest soll zeigen, wie widerstandsfähig die Faltmechanik des Smartphones bei intensiver Nutzung ist. Eine spezielle Testmaschine öffnet und schließt das Gerät fortlaufend. Inzwischen wurden mehr als 451.000 Faltvorgänge absolviert.

iPhone Duo: Erste Veränderungen nach 390.000 Faltvorgängen

Nach Angaben von CNET zeigten sich die ersten Auffälligkeiten bereits bei rund 390.000 Öffnungs- und Schließvorgängen. Zu diesem Zeitpunkt fühlte sich das Scharnier zunehmend locker an.

Bei etwa 440.300 Faltvorgängen veränderte sich das Verhalten der Mechanik dann deutlicher. Das Smartphone erreichte beim automatischen Öffnen nicht mehr seine vollständig aufgeklappte Position, bevor die Testmaschine den nächsten Schließvorgang einleitete.

Zuvor hatte sich das Display nach dem Zurückziehen des Öffnungsmechanismus noch selbstständig bis zur Endposition bewegt. Dieses Verhalten blieb schließlich aus.

Das iPhone Duo öffnet sich inzwischen nur noch bis auf etwa fünf bis zehn Grad an die vollständig aufgeklappte Position heran. Von Hand lässt sich das Gerät allerdings weiterhin vollständig öffnen.

Auch das zuvor wahrnehmbare Einrasten der Mechanik bleibt mittlerweile aus.

Display bislang ohne erkennbare Schäden

Trotz der Veränderungen am Scharnier funktioniert das getestete iPhone Duo nach Angaben von CNET weiterhin.

Das faltbare OLED-Display zeigt bislang keine sichtbaren Risse oder andere erkennbare Beschädigungen. Auch die übrigen Funktionen des Smartphones sind weiterhin verfügbar.

Das Gerät kann außerdem noch in verschiedenen Öffnungswinkeln gehalten werden. Ein vollständiger Ausfall der Faltmechanik ist somit bislang nicht eingetreten.

CNET hat das Smartphone deshalb nicht aus der Testmaschine genommen. Der Dauertest wird fortgesetzt, um festzustellen, nach wie vielen Faltvorgängen tatsächlich ein relevanter Defekt auftritt.

Test läuft bis zum technischen Ausfall

Für den Belastungstest hat CNET mehrere Kriterien definiert, bei deren Eintreten das Gerät als ausgefallen gilt.

Dazu gehören unter anderem ein vollständiger Funktionsverlust, Probleme bei der Erkennung des Öffnungszustands durch die Sensoren sowie ein Ausfall des Displays.

Die bislang beobachtete Lockerung des Scharniers erfüllt diese Kriterien offenbar noch nicht.

Der Test wird deshalb fortgesetzt, obwohl die Faltmechanik bereits Veränderungen aufweist.

Apple selbst hat bislang keine Angaben dazu veröffentlicht, auf wie viele Faltvorgänge das Scharnier des iPhone Duo ausgelegt ist. Auch Ergebnisse möglicher interner Belastungstests hat der Konzern nicht öffentlich gemacht.

Samsung-Display bestand Test mit 500.000 Faltvorgängen

Das iPhone Duo verwendet faltbare OLED-Panels von Samsung Display. Der südkoreanische Hersteller verfügt bereits über umfangreiche Erfahrungen mit Displays für faltbare Smartphones.

Das im Samsung Galaxy Z Fold7 eingesetzte Display bestand einen unabhängig zertifizierten Belastungstest mit 500.000 Faltvorgängen.

Allerdings ist nicht davon auszugehen, dass Apple zwangsläufig ein technisch identisches Standarddisplay verwendet. Die Konstruktion und die Anforderungen an das Panel können sich zwischen den Geräten unterscheiden.

Die bisherigen Ergebnisse des CNET-Tests deuten dennoch darauf hin, dass das Display des iPhone Duo eine vergleichbare Belastung überstehen könnte.

Für die tatsächliche Lebensdauer eines faltbaren Smartphones ist allerdings nicht nur die Widerstandsfähigkeit des Bildschirms entscheidend. Auch die mechanische Konstruktion des Scharniers spielt eine wesentliche Rolle.

So lange würde das Scharnier des Duo mit 450.000 Öffnungen durchhalten

Wie hoch die bisher erreichte Belastung ausfällt, zeigt eine rechnerische Einordnung.

Wird ein faltbares Smartphone täglich 100-mal geöffnet und geschlossen, entsprechen 450.000 Faltvorgänge einer Nutzungsdauer von rund 12,3 Jahren.

Bei 200 Faltvorgängen pro Tag wären es immer noch gut sechs Jahre.

Diese Berechnung berücksichtigt allerdings ausschließlich die Zahl der mechanischen Bewegungen. Alterungsprozesse, Temperaturschwankungen, Staub, Feuchtigkeit und andere Einflüsse des Alltags werden durch einen solchen Dauertest nicht vollständig abgebildet.

title: Don’t Be So Surprised That Mississippi Turned Blue
subtitle: senator ever elected by Mississippians, traces his lineage in the state back seven generations, to when the nation was forging its foundation on th…
feedText: Scott Colom, the first Black U.S. He waged a campaign set on showing that “Mississippi matters,” which many registered more as a question than a declaration, doubting whether a Black man and a Democrat could win the seat. During the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history, his campaign coffers were empty compared with Democrats in other battleground races. articleBody:
Scott Colom, the first Black U.S. senator ever elected by Mississippians, traces his lineage in the state back seven generations, to when the nation was forging its foundation on the backs of stolen Black people. He waged a campaign set on showing that “Mississippi matters,” which many registered more as a question than a declaration, doubting whether a Black man and a Democrat could win the seat. During the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history, his campaign coffers were empty compared with Democrats in other battleground races. Finally victorious on Veterans Day, he credited the state’s civil-rights titans and local people who work without an expectation of recognition for carrying on the “Mississippi faith tradition” of having hope, even—or perhaps especially—in dark chapters.

Many Americans might be surprised that Colom flipped what’s long been a deeply red seat. But this win is the product of decades of uphill, incremental, thankless, and overlooked labor powered by an ancestral charge and a conviction to reclaim Mississippi. My late stepfather, Obbie Riley, a five-term Democratic county supervisor in Mississippi, was among those who undertook that fight, although he didn’t live long enough to see its results. The state’s “faith tradition” that Colom evoked is as much about prayer as it is about remembering generations of bloodshed in Mississippi, where Black voting rights were redeemed by those who could only dream of what Colom has now achieved: finally turning his home state blue.

“There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” Colom said during his victory speech Wednesday night. “And that is another tradition of our state. There’s so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible.”

That faith, and the hard work that must accompany it, was something Colom learned in his household, where he and his twin brother were reared by now-retired Judge Dorothy Colom, the first Black person to be elected to her region’s chancery court, and Wilbur Colom, an attorney who was once a Republican. Scott built on this pedigree, attending the University of Wisconsin to study law and returning home to the Columbus area, in the east-central pocket of the state, not far from the Alabama line. There he became the youngest and the first African American justice-court judge in Lowndes County, in 2011, and then Columbus’s first African American city prosecutor, in 2013. Later he took a bolder step, campaigning for district attorney in his early 30s.

[Adam Serwer: Even where MAGA won, MAGA lost]

If Columbus were anywhere else, it might be described as a natural incubator for a Democratic U.S. senator. It is a college town, home to the state’s women’s university; it’s also a vertex of a region known as “The Golden Triangle,” which is anchored by Mississippi State University and an Air Force base in Starkville. Colom ran for district attorney in 2015 as a reform candidate—and unseated a 27-year incumbent who’d defended debunked medical-examiner analyses that had led to multiple false convictions that were later overturned. Colom has been the region’s top cop for more than a decade; he instituted restorative justice and counseling for gun-violence survivors, among other reforms. In 2020, days after George Floyd was murdered, Mississippi’s attorney general suddenly dropped a police-shooting case that Colom had transferred to the state in 2016. Colom was outspoken about it, making parts of the case file public and expressing regret for handing the case over.

History is never fully in the rearview in Mississippi, and that was evident throughout the Colom campaign. On the day before he delivered his victory speech, at Tougaloo College, a historically Black school with a rich civil-rights history, Colom held a press conference wearing a mocha-brown hoodie that bore a quote from the civil-rights organizer Bob Moses: When you’re in Mississippi, the rest of America doesn’t seem real. And when you’re in the rest of America, Mississippi doesn’t seem real. Moses directed Freedom Summer, the 1964 effort to recruit hundreds of white college students to Mississippi to help open Freedom Schools, or voter-registration-and-education sites meant to overcome the ridicule, violence, and other tactics the state used to keep Black voters off the rolls. At the time, the state had the lowest Black voter-registration numbers, despite being the Blackest state in the U.S.

Training for the college students was under way when members of the Ku Klux Klan burned down Mt. Zion United Methodist Church in Philadelphia, Mississippi, after beating parishioners suspected of holding civil-rights meetings. Michael Schwerner and James Chaney, organizers who had done grassroots work at Mt. Zion, knew they had to leave Freedom Summer training in Ohio to check on the community. Andrew Goodman, a college student who volunteered for Freedom Summer, joined them on his first trip to Mississippi. On the afternoon of June 21, as the trio made their way through the center of Philadelphia, the deputy sheriff, a Klansman, pulled them over and arrested them. When they were released after nightfall, a group of Klansmen and law enforcement kidnapped them, killed them, and buried them in an earthen dam in Neshoba County, where an FBI search located them 44 days later.

This past summer, Colom made a campaign stop at the Neshoba County Fair, where politicians frequently stump. Ronald Reagan spoke there during his 1980 presidential campaign, emphasizing his belief in states’ rights, which many interpreted as a dog whistle, given the proximity to where the three civil-rights workers had been slain. Colom’s father worked for Reagan’s transition team. In a 1981 interview with The Daily Mississippian, the University of Mississippi’s student newspaper, Wilbur Colom criticized some of Reagan’s policies and said that the GOP of the ’50s and ’60s had been deficient in its support for civil-rights legislation, but that Black voters’ commitment to the Democratic Party shouldn’t be automatic either.

Wilbur’s son ran a campaign with a complementary refrain: Why should Mississippi automatically be considered a Republican stronghold, especially when Democrats have chipped away at GOP control in statewide elections over the past decade? When my stepfather died in September, he was the lone Black person and Democrat serving as a Neshoba County supervisor. And although that set him apart, he’s remembered for how he sifted through disagreements to move forward, even if the ideological overlap with his colleagues was the size of a grain of sand. Throughout his campaign, Colom likewise touted that he would work with anyone, Republican or otherwise; he even visited a Trump rally and spoke with people waiting in line. There’s a Mississippi brand of bipartisanship, one my stepdad practiced, that’s a mainstay especially in rural areas, where people of difference have found commonality even amid bitter political and racial tensions.

Colom’s win was propelled by grassroots organizing to register voters, get them to the polls, and, in some cases, help them return to certify or cure provisional ballots. The senator-elect outraised his opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, in the last quarter of the campaign (approximately $1.45 million to $864,000), but that was nothing compared with the money pouring in for other Democratic Senate candidates. Colom’s campaign had a “rich message but a poor treasury,” Representative Bennie Thompson said at the Tougaloo victory party, where he introduced the senator-elect.

With seemingly nothing to lose, Colom infused a little bit of fun into his campaign, producing a series of ads that showcased his sense of humor. One, called “Sinators,” parodied the Mississippi-based movie Sinners using Colom’s identical twin brother. In it, a Hyde-Smith look-alike asks for just one more chance to keep everything in Mississippi the way it is. Hyde-Smith, whose parents sent her to a segregation academy as a child, was caught on camera in 2018 saying of a supporter standing beside her that if he “invited me to a public hanging, I’d be on the front row”—in the state where more known lynchings occurred than in any other. (She later said that the remark was an “exaggerated expression of regard.”) She conceded the race after it was called on Wednesday, and congratulated Colom on his victory. The moment had a karmic quality: After President Biden nominated Colom to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in 2022, Hyde-Smith single-handedly blocked him from the lifetime appointment, even though other statewide Republicans supported him for the role.

For a time, it looked as if the election results might face legal challenges. During the week-long vote counting, Hyde-Smith was asked about the possibility of fraud in the election and said, “There’s always irregularities.” In the summer of 2025, Mississippi shifted tens of thousands of voters to “inactive” status based on data from the credit-reporting agency Experian. DeSoto County, home to the white-flight suburbs of Memphis, inactivated more than 15,000 voters, more than anywhere else in the state. On Election Day, lines there lagged, and polling stations ran low on affidavit ballots. Colom won the county with about 53 percent of the vote; Hyde-Smith had won the county in her previous two elections.

The first time the Department of Justice used the now-gutted 1965 Voting Rights Act to protect white voters happened in Colom’s district, in Noxubee County, in 2005; Wilbur Colom represented the defendant in the case. A decade later, around the time that Scott Colom was running for district attorney, a DOJ lawyer from the 2005 case filed a lawsuit alleging issues with the Noxubee voter rolls. Instead of undertaking a costly fight, the county entered a consent decree that required a period of scrutinized voter-roll management. Noxubee and Lowndes, another county in Colom’s district, also saw voter inactivations surge in the months before the 2026 midterms. This living history is another reason many doubted whether Colom, or any Black senatorial candidate, could make it to Washington.

Political pundits have already compared this moment to the Barack Obama elections, which saw high Black voter turnout in Mississippi and elsewhere. Nadia Colom—the wife of the senator-elect, a real-estate agent, and former executive director of the Golden Triangle Boys and Girls Club—said in her speech on Wednesday that people have been calling her “Mississippi’s Michelle,” referring to the former first lady. “While it’s an honor, really and truly, to be seen in that light, what really means the most to me is that I get to be called Mississippi’s,” she said.

[Read: Why Black voters abandoned Trump]

Colom’s campaign rightly touts him as the first Black U.S. senator to be elected by Mississippians. Mississippi sent two Black senators—Hiram Revels, the nation’s first Black senator, and later Blanche Bruce—to Washington at a time when they were selected by state legislators. Black men also served as secretary of state in Mississippi for nearly a decade after the Civil War. In 1870, 14 percent of the state Senate and 47 percent of the state House of Representatives were made up of Black men. By 1874, nearly 80 percent of the state House was Black. Because Reconstruction showed such promise in Mississippi, the backlash that followed was orchestrated, acute, and violent.

A defining feature of Mississippi history is that white violence directly triggered an exodus. One historian estimates that from 1914 to 1920, during the Great Migration, one in five of the Black migrants leaving the South for economic opportunity, safety, dignity, and more came from Mississippi. White Mississippians waged yet more violence against Black folks who stayed, assassinating Medgar Evers, sickening and fatiguing Fannie Lou Hamer, and brutalizing everyday citizens into strange fruit. The remnants of that targeted violence are still visible today in the state’s stark inequality and lack of opportunity for Black Mississippians.

But Colom’s campaign challenges the narrative that Mississippi should be defined through the lens of white harm, and that those with aspirations are better off leaving. On Wednesday night, Nadia Colom said to her and Scott’s twin girls, eighth-generation Mississippians, that she hoped the race reinforced the family motto to never quit, a value instilled in their father, who passed it to them. Persistence is a precious inheritance in a state that often ranks dead-last in indicators of prosperity, livelihood, health, well-being, and education. Scott Colom didn’t quit when donors wouldn’t answer the phone, when fewer than 10 people showed up at his first town hall, when it took eight days to rightfully claim his victory. For 200 years and counting, his ancestors didn’t quit on Mississippi, toiling and resisting on the lands that he traversed during his campaign. Now he is reaping the reward of remaining.

title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
subtitle: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games, and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel.
feedText: At Summer Game Fest 2026, we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reesta…
articleBody:
The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games, and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel.

At Summer Game Fest 2026, we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong?

Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years.

Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2's pure survival horror to look forward to.

Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason.

Another glorious day in the Corps

(Image credit: Daybreak Game Company)
Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat.

This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running.

(Image credit: Daybreak Game Company)
All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode.

At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away.

Game over, man

(Image credit: Daybreak Game Company)
There are still some scares hiding in here, though, ready to make complacent players jump out of their seats. Special Xenomorphs have tricks to pounce on distracted players, throwing chaos into the middle of their carefully coordinated rain of fire. Others have the ability to spit from afar, breaking tight defenses that count on the Xenos' predictable tactics from other games and the movies.

It's been 40 years since Aliens first graced the big screen, but Fireteam Elite 2 manages to refresh that mix of horror and action well enough, despite sharing much of its bones with the original game. But the disturbing lack of polish threatens to undo Cold Iron Studios' best ideas.

Those ideas include more varied enemies, which can disrupt almost any tried-and-tested team composition, and even a late-game class that rewards an extensive knowledge of the game by letting veterans pick weapons from all over the roster to create a custom loadout.

(Image credit: Daybreak Game Company)
These playful creative swings somewhat offset the frustration caused by glitched objectives, enemy AI that often goes off the rails, and performance issues that have often given me flashbacks to its predecessor's worst moments on PS4. Sometimes, you can just tell when six extra months would've done a game a lot of good, and it's obvious that Fireteam Elite 2 will be in a much better place by spring.

That said, its loose and confident approach to design is rare to see when dealing with games that adapt well-established IPs like Alien.

Recent Star Wars games have achieved just that, and even if Fireteam Elite 2 misses some of its shots and has faced more initial trouble than the USCM's first incursion on LV-426, it's safe to say its heart and mind are in the right place. No one can take that away from the devs. Show me another modern Alien video game that allows you to zap Xenomorphs to death with a big cannon or to hold them off with combat drones.

We've seen developers win uphill battles before, and we know for a fact the huge Alien fandom is as enduring as the deadly extraterrestrials, so Daybreak and Cold Iron have a chance to turn things around and solidify Fireteam Elite 2 as the iterative but satisfying sequel it actually is.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is available now for PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. A Nintendo Switch 2 version is coming in 2027.

We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, REI’s annual Holiday Sale, which runs through November 23rd, is worth checking out.

As usual, the outdoor retailer is offering discounts on everything from smartwatches to camping equipment. In some cases, we’re seeing some of the lowest prices we’ve seen on our favorite wearables, including Garmin’s Forerunner 570, while gadgets like the InReach Mini 3 are also receiving sizable discounts. REI members can also use promo code HOLIDAY2026 to save 20 percent on one full-price item, plus an additional 20 percent on one REI Outlet item.

To save you time, we’ve sifted through the deluge of discounts to find an assortment of deals we recommend here at The Verge. We’ve also noted when competing retailers are offering lower prices on the same items, so you can be sure you’re getting the best deal possible.

Smartwatches and fitness tech

Garmin Forerunner 570

Garmin’s Forerunner 570 features a bright OLED display, skin temperature sensors, and a built-in speaker and microphone for taking calls. It also offers multiband GPS, personalized training plans, and up to 11 days of battery life.

Where to Buy:

$549.99 $449.99 at Amazon

$549.99 $449.99 at Best Buy

$550 $449.99 at REI

Garmin Venu 4

Garmin’s Venu 4 is geared toward the average athlete, offering heart rate alerts, detailed sleep insights, guided meditation, and a wheelchair mode. It also introduces caffeine and alcohol tracking, along with Garmin Coach, which tailors workouts to your fitness history, sleep, and recovery.

Where to Buy:

$549.93 at Amazon

$549.99 at Best Buy

$550 $449.99 at REI

REI, Amazon, and Best Buy are also selling the Garmin Lily 2 Active for $249.99 ($50 off), which is its lowest price to date. The stylish smartwatch is a great budget-friendly Garmin, especially for people with smaller wrists. Like the standard Lily 2, it offers basic fitness tracking, notifications, and up to five days of battery life; however, the so-called “Active” model adds a physical button, built-in GPS, and support for more sports tracking. Read our Lily 2 review.

The Garmin Vivoactive 6 has returned to its all-time low of $249.99 ($50 off) at Amazon, Walmart, and REI. The fitness watch offers up to 11 days of battery life and tracks a range of workouts, including walking, running, cycling, HIIT, golf, and more. It also provides extensive health monitoring, including wrist-based heart rate detection, menstrual cycle and pregnancy tracking, and a customizable morning report that summarizes helpful health-related info. However, it lacks ECG compatibility, though it does have a slightly slimmer profile than its predecessor.

Garmin Fenix 8

The Garmin Fenix 8 is a premium multisport watch that features a speaker, mic, and on-device assistant for calls, timers, and voice commands. It also offers elite battery life, dual-frequency GPS, and robust sensors. Read our review.

Where to Buy:

$999.99 $749.99 at Amazon (43mm)

$1099.99 $749.99 at Walmart (47mm)

$1099.99 $849.99 at REI (47mm)

The Wahoo Kickr V6 Smart Trainer is on sale at REI for $679.99 ($170 off). Like the more affordable Kickr Core 2 we covered in July, the Kickr V6 turns your existing bike into an indoor exercise bike, with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for pairing with apps like Zwift. However, the higher-end trainer offers up to 2,200W of resistance and can replicate inclines of up to 20 percent, compared to the Core 2’s 1,800W and 16 percent. It also provides more accurate power measurements and is designed so that indoor rides feel more natural.

Phone accessories and entertainment

EcoFlow Rapid Magnetic Power Bank

EcoFlow’s Rapid Magnetic Power Bank is a 10,000mAh Qi2 battery that can snap to the back of your device if you’re using a newer iPhone or select Android devices, thus supplying it with up to 15W of power. It also includes a built-in USB-C cable that can provide up to 65W of power to larger devices, including a 13-inch MacBook Air.

Where to Buy:

$90 $66.93 at REI

If you own an older iPhone with a Lightning port, you can grab InfinityLab’s InstantGo 10,000 Power Bank for $41.93 (about $28 off) at REI. The portable battery features a 10,000mAh capacity and a built-in Lightning cable, making it a solid all-in-one option for days when you won’t be near an outlet. It also supports passthrough charging, so you can charge your phone and the power bank at the same time.

DJI’s Osmo Mobile 8 is on sale for around $128.99 ($21 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $10 shy of its best price to date. The smartphone gimbal supports 360-degree horizontal rotation and Apple’s DockKit, which allows the gimbal to track and follow pets and people across a wider range of camera apps. This discounted Advanced Tracking Combo also includes a multifunctional module for tracking people and pets, as well as a built-in tripod and extension rod that make it easier to film yourself without someone behind the camera.

Soundcore Liberty 5

The Soundcore Liberty 5 feature adaptive noise cancellation and support for Dolby Audio, along with six swappable tips so you can find the right fit. They also sport an IP55 rating for water and dust resistance and can last up to 48 hours with the included charging case.

Where to Buy:

$129.99 $89.99 at Amazon

$129.99 $89.99 at Walmart

$130 $89.99 at REI

You can buy Soundcore’s AeroFit 2 for $79.99 ($20 off) at REI, Amazon, and Best Buy, which is $2 shy of their lowest price to date. Their open-ear design lets you listen to music while staying vigilant in your surroundings; they also feature adjustable ear hooks for a secure fit, IP55 water and dust resistance, and up to 42 hours of battery life with the included charging case.

Anker Nebula P1 projector

Anker’s Nebula P1 is a portable 1080p projector with built-in Google TV and two detachable Bluetooth speakers that deliver better sound than many all-in-one portable projectors. It offers 650 ANSI lumens of brightness and can project images up to 180 inches, while the speakers last up to 20 hours on a charge.

Where to Buy:

$799 $599.99 at Amazon

$799 $599 at Soundcore

$799 $699.99 at REI

Communication and safety gear

Garmin InReach Mini 3 Plus

The Mini 3 Plus is identical to the standard model in that it allows you to stay connected while off the grid; however, it also features an audible siren and the ability to send photos and voice messages, in addition to standard texts.

Where to Buy:

$499.99 $399.99 at Amazon

$499.99 $399.99 at REI

$499.99 $399.99 at Garmin

Garmin’s base InReach Mini 3 is available from REI, Amazon, and Garmin for around $349 ($100 off), nearly matching its lowest price to date. Like the Mini 2, the rugged, palm-sized satellite communicator lets you send texts, share your location, check the weather, and trigger SOS alerts when you’re off the grid, all while offering battery life that can outlast your average smartphone. Unlike the prior version, though, it features a color touchscreen, which makes it easier to navigate menus and bang out messages.

Garmin’s InReach Messenger Plus is also on sale at REI, Amazon, and direct from Garmin for $299.99 ($100 off), matching its best price to date. The subscription-based Plus model provides satellite connectivity and access to emergency services like the aforementioned InReach Mini 3, except it can also send photos and audio clips in addition to standard text messages.

The Chapter MIPS Bike Helmet is on sale starting at around $112.39 ($41 off) at REI, which nearly matches its best price to date. The lightweight helmet features a hidden PopLock for securing it with a U-lock or chain. It also has a sleek visor and a Micro-USB taillight with 30 lumens of brightness, one that automatically turns on when magnetically attached to the helmet.

Garmin’s Varia RTL515 Radar Taillight is on sale at REI and Amazon for $149.99 ($50 off), which is about $10 less than its all-time low. The headlight combines a bright LED light with a rearview radar that, when paired with a compatible device, warns you of cars approaching from behind from up to 153 yards away.

BCA Tracker 3 Plus Avalanche Transceiver

The Tracker 3 Plus is a pocketable, lightweight avalanche beacon designed to help locate people buried in snow. It features a real-time display, lights to guide searchers, and tools for finding multiple people. It also comes with a harness and batteries.

Where to Buy:

$349.95 $279.89 at REI

Camping and travel gear

Exped MegaMat Duo

The MegaMat Duo is a four-inch, self-inflating mattress that’s become one of our favorites thanks to its extra-wide design. It uses a combination of open-cell polyurethane foam and generous padding for comfort, which helps keep you warm when temperatures dip. It also makes for a stellar air mattress for guests.

Where to Buy:

$399.95 $299.89 at REI (medium)

$549.95 $412.39 at REI (queen)

$449.95 $337.39 at REI (long wide)

A small chair is nice to have for lounging by the campfire, and REI’s Flexlite Camp Chair is a great option now that it’s down to around $67.39 (about $22 off) in multiple colors at REI. It features an aluminum frame, a stable four-leg design, and a ripstop polyester seat with water and stain resistance. When you’re done, it also folds down quickly into a drawstring bag, so you can throw it in your car.

Kelty Low Loveseat

The Kelty Low Loveseat is a sturdy, low-profile camp chair built for two. It features a steel frame, a padded seat, and extra-large cup holders for your drinks or gear. It also includes a padded roll-tote storage bag, making it easy to transport when it’s folded down.

Where to Buy:

$149.95 $112.39 at REI

$149.95 $119.96 at Backcountry

REI is currently selling its Magma 30 Sleeping Bag in a variety of sizes starting at $243.93 ($105 off). The bag uses 850-fill-power, water-resistant down for warmth and weighs under 20 ounces, depending on the size, making it a great budget pick if you’re looking to get into ultralight backpacking. It also includes a hood to help retain heat, extra room around the feet, and a terrific zipper design that’s less likely to snag when you’re crawling in or out.

REI Siesta Hooded 20 Sleeping Bag

The Siesta prioritizes comfort with a roomy rectangular shape that gives you space to stretch out. The synthetic sleeping bag features an insulated hood — one that’s spacious enough to accommodate a real pillow — along with multiple zipper configurations so you can vent your feet or fully unzip it into a quilt-like blanket.

Where to Buy:

$149 $111.69 at REI (medium)

$159 $119.19 at REI (long)

Rumpl Original Puffy Blanket

Rumpl’s classic lightweight blanket features synthetic insulation for warmth, a weather-resistant outer shell, and a stuff sack. It also comes in an array of attractive designs and pairs with Rumpl’s Cape Clip, so you can wear it hands-free.

Where to Buy:

$99.95 $74.89 at REI (one-person)

$99.95 $74.96 at Rumpl (one-person)

$199.95 $149.89 at REI (two-person)

Osprey’s Atmos AG 65 Pack is on sale in several colors and size configurations for around $258.93 ($112 off) at REI, which is one of the lowest prices we’ve seen. The 65-liter pack — which remains a go-to option for The Verge’s own Brandon Widder — is loaded with all sorts of bells and whistles, including an integrated rain cover, a floating top lid, and plenty of compression straps. The hallmark, though, is the ventilation system, which leverages a 3D-suspended mesh for comfort and breathability, making it a great pick for multi-day trips.

REI’s Ruckpack Waist Pack is on sale for $33.69 ($12 off) at REI, which is one of the best prices we’ve seen as of late. Made from a water-repellent material, this small adjustable bag can be worn around your waist or across your body and features three interior pockets for keeping your essentials organized.

Sea to Summit Hanging Toiletry Bag

Sea to Summit’s small toiletry bag lets you keep all of your essentials close at hand for weekend getaways. It features a water–resistant fabric and a convenient hanging hook, along with internal mesh pockets so you can quickly find whatever it is you need.

Where to Buy:

$49.95 $37.39 at REI

The JetBoil Stash Cooking System is a compact, lightweight cooking system that’s currently down to $123.69 (about $41 off) at REI, which is one of the lowest prices we’ve seen all year. It features a standalone stove with a titanium burner and a 0.8-liter cooking pot, allowing you to boil water or heat food at your campsite. The pot comes with a lid and a pour handle, too, and everything can be stowed inside the pot when you’re finished, making it exceptionally easy to pack up.

Sea to Summit Aeros Premium Pillow

Sea to Summit’s lightweight, inflatable camping pillow features a soft memory foam layer, adjustable firmness, and a curved design that cradles your head. It’s also quick to inflate and includes patches to keep it from sliding while you sleep.

Where to Buy:

$54.95 $41.19 at REI (Regular)

$59.95 $44.89 at REI (Large)

$69.95 $52.39 at REI (XL)

You can buy the ultralight Nemo Tensor in multiple sizes starting at REI for $131.93 (about $88 off). Designed for backpacking, the four-season sleeping pad offers 3.5 inches of cushioning and insulation to keep you warm in colder conditions, with a 5.4 R-value. The nylon construction is also relatively quiet, which, frankly, isn’t the case with many of the camping pads we’ve used over the years.

Nemo’s Stargaze Evo-X is on sale for $99.99 ($80 off) at REI, which is a great price for the surprisingly portable camping chair. The plush, versatile chair automatically reclines when you lean back, making it ideal for relaxing around the campsite (and stargazing). It also features a padded headrest, two cupholders, and a folding frame. And did we mention it swings? Because it swings.

REI’s Wonderland Cot is down to $187.39 ($62 off) at REI. The foldable cot — which is designed more for car camping than anything else — features a spacious, padded sleeping surface, an adjustable backrest, and a sturdy aluminum and steel frame that supports up to 300 pounds. The new version also comes with a webbing carrying strap, making it easier to lug around than prior models.

Headlamps and lighting

Mpowerd Luci Solar String Lights: Color

Mpowerd’s solar-powered string lights are perfect for camping or a backyard shindig. The 18-foot string can display six colors and last up to 15 hours on a single charge; the case also doubles as a charger, allowing you to top off your phone in a pinch.

Where to Buy:

$54.95 $19.83 at REI

Black Diamond’s Spot, the newer version of the Spot 400 headlamp, is on sale for $47.89 ($12 off) at REI. It offers up to 450 lumens of adjustable brightness, up from 400, along with red night vision and an IPX7 water-resistance rating. You can also choose to power it with standard AAA batteries or Black Diamond’s rechargeable battery.

The Petzl Tikka is on sale at REI for $18.77 (about $16 off). The basic headlamp is a great option that features a max output of 350 lumens, tilt functionality, and an IPX4 rating, making it safe to use in light rain. It also features a lock function that prevents it from accidentally turning on when packed.

Black Diamond Moji Plus Lantern

The Moji Plus offers 200 lumens of warm, dimmable light and adjustable brightness, along with an IPX4 rating for water resistance. It also features a double-hook design and the same dual-fuel tech as the Spot 400 Headlamp, meaning you can use it with standard AAAs or Black Diamond’s rechargeable BD 1500 Li-ion battery.

Where to Buy:

$34.95 $29.95 at Amazon

$34.95 $27.89 at REI

The Nite Ize Radiant 314 — which is currently down to $23.77 (about $22 off) at REI — provides 314 lumens of brightness, an impact-resistant design, and an IPX4 rating for water resistance. The rechargeable lantern can also last up to 96 hours on a single charge, while the built-in power bank can provide an extra boost of power to your phone in a pinch.

Luminaid’s Max 2-in-1 Power Lantern, which now inflates with a simple twist, is available for $47.19 (about $13 off) at REI. The nifty lantern delivers up to 200 lumens of light and lasts up to 50 hours; it also doubles as a portable phone charger, recharges either via solar power or USB, and folds flat.

title: Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life
subtitle: Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transien…
feedText: And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives. If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum. “Love quells fear,” Octavia Butler wrote in contemplating creativity, “and a sweet and powerful positive obsession blunts pain, diverts rage, and engages each of us in the greatest, the most intense of our chosen struggles.” Our highly cli…
articleBody:
Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives. And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives.

If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum. “Love quells fear,” Octavia Butler wrote in contemplating creativity, “and a sweet and powerful positive obsession blunts pain, diverts rage, and engages each of us in the greatest, the most intense of our chosen struggles.” Our highly clinical culture, with its tendency to pathologize the tendrils of personality that make us who we are, regards obsession as unambiguously negative — something that kidnaps us from the actuality of life. And yet all the creative energy that has given us our greatest works of art and most revolutionary breakthroughs in science has sprung from such a “powerful positive obsession.”

Susan Orlean takes up this question in her 1994 classic The Orchid Thief: A True Story of Beauty and Obsession (public library). One answer to what we long for in our existential longing, she posits, may be “to know what it feels like to care about something passionately” — to have an obsession, something very particular to which you pay rigorous and rapturous attention.

When she asks her protagonist what it is about orchids he finds so irresistible, how it is they are the animating passion of his life, he shrugs:

Oh, mystery, beauty, unknowability, I suppose… I think the real reason is that life has no meaning. I mean, no obvious meaning. You wake up, you go to work, you do stuff. I think everybody’s always looking for something a little unusual that can preoccupy them and help pass the time.

Often, it is not we who find that unusual something but it that finds us, jolts us awake from the stupor of near-living. Considering her own obsession with telling the story of the orchid thief, which had begun with a random article she read in a newspaper on a random day and ended up consuming years of her life, she observes how these obsessions take hold of us:

[It begins with] some glimpse of life that expands like those Japanese paper balls you drop in water and then after a moment they bloom into flowers, and the flower is so marvelous that you can’t believe there was a time when all you saw in front of you was a paper ball and a glass of water.

Art from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days. (Available as a print and as stationery cards.)

As Susan finds herself traveling through the vastness of Florida in the footsteps of the orchid thief, she comes to see these obsessions as our most powerful antidote to the hollow feeling of meaninglessness that visits upon every life — against the overwhelming bigness of life, we have the saving grace of smallness:

The land was marble-smooth and it rolled without a pucker to the horizon. My eyes grazed across the green band of ground and the blue bowl of sky and then lingered on a dead tire, a bird in flight, an old fence, a rusted barrel. Hardly any cars came toward me, and I saw no one in the rearview mirror the entire time. I passed so many vacant acres and looked past them to so many more vacant acres and looked ahead and behind at the empty road and up at the empty sky; the sheer bigness of the world made me feel lonely to the bone. The world is so huge that people are always getting lost in it. There are too many ideas and things and people, too many directions to go. I was starting to believe that the reason it matters to care passionately about something is that it whittles the world down to a more manageable size. It makes the world seem not huge and empty but full of possibility.

Nothing counterbalances our helpless givens and shapes our lives more powerfully than our relationship to possibility. To be overwhelmed is to be paralyzed by possibility. To be obsessed it to be catalyzed by it. Whatever the obsession is one of collecting or creating, whatever form it takes — orchids or oboe, birds or baking, writing or trapeze — it is a way of centering into our only task here: to fill our allotted days with maximum aliveness.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)

articleBody:
Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that."

SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster.

The giant Starship rocket, a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history.

The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned. Instead of returning to its launch tower to be caught mid-air by the tower's metal "chopstick" arms, however, the rocket veered offshore and detonated its flight termination system. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that a guidance issue appeared to be the cause.

The Super Heavy first-stage booster of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 rocket explodes during splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico after launching its Ship upper stage to orbit from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future)

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.View Deal

"We were initially 'go' for a catch," Huot said during live commentary on Friday, about seven hours into the mission. "But in the later stages of the coast, the booster aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected, and that put it into its contingency landing offshore." Super Heavy exploded a few feet above the waves of the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

GNC is short for Guidance and Navigation Control, a criticial system used by rockets to control their flight and ensure they remain on their planned course. Such a system is vital for any landing attempt by a Starship Super Heavy or Ship upper stage to ensure the vehicle returns to its landing site safely and doesn't veer off course to damage SpaceX's Starbase or surrounding populated areas.

In an update during SpaceX's Flight 15 coverage on Saturday, however, Huot said that Super Heavy's GNC system actually performed well.

"I did a disservice to our booster GNC guys last night," Huot said. "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, [it] detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location."

SpaceX is "still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that," he added on Saturday.

You can follow our Starship Flight 15 live updates for the latest on the mission.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy Booster's explosive offshore landing abort in pictures. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Steve Spaleta/Space.com/Future)
Super Heavy is powered by a cluster of 33 Raptor rocket engines that fire simultaneously during liftoff to send the 41-story Starship megarocket into orbit. During Friday's launch, all 33 engines fired as planned for the ascent, Huot said.

One engine did drop out after stage separation, when Super Heavy dropped away from Ship and flipped over for a "boostback" burn to begin its trip back to Earth, Huot said on Friday.

"We had 32 out of the 33 booster engines lit for boostback, which started sending it back here to the launch site," he added.

A close look at the 33 Raptor engines firing simultaneously to launch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission into orbit. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future)
That firing was followed by the booster's landing burn. In SpaceX's launch video, Super Heavy can be seen activating 13 of its Raptor engines as planned, followed by the abort and the booster steering itself to a contingency landing zone in Gulf waters.

"It did that hover, cut the engines off, the FTS — the flight termination system — triggered, and it splashed down in the water," Huot said on Friday. (The FTS is designed to destroy a booster in the event of an emergency.)

As its name suggests, Starship Flight 15 is SpaceX's 15th test flight of the giant rocket, but it will be the first to attempt to catch a Ship upper stage with the chopsticks. SpaceX has successfully caught Super Heavy boosters on three test flights to date.

Flight 15's Ship vehicle is in good health and will orbit Earth a total of 14 times before landing back at its launch pad in Starbase at around 4:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT) today, if all goes well.

"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground-tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said in Friday's mission update. (Flight 15 hauled 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, and a few of those spacecraft carried cameras for heat-shield inspection.)

SpaceX designed Starship to be fully reusable, with the company banking on that reusability to make it an affordable heavy-lift booster capable of a wide range of missions to low Earth orbit, the moon and eventually Mars.

NASA has picked Starship as one of two commercial landers to carry Artemis astronauts to the moon in 2028, and SpaceX sees the rocket as vital to building out a 100,000 constellation of Starlink V3 internet satellites, as well as a new AI data center network in orbit called Starmind.

But first, SpaceX has to successfully land a Starship upper stage from orbit. That's the next step for Flight 15.

Huot said that flight controllers will make one last check at the 20-hour mark in the mission to decide whether to proceed with the landing at Starbase or make an "early return" splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.

That final check is expected by about 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT). Space.com's Starship Flight 15 landing livestream will begin at that time, and will be carried on our live updates page, Space.com homepage and our VideoFromSpace YouTube page.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:50 a.m. ET on Nov. 14 with the latest information from SpaceX's Dan Huot, who clarified that the booster tower-catch abort was not caused by a GNC issue.

articleBody:
Bei ChatGPT, Gemini und Co. ist das Prinzip längst bekannt: Ein Grundkontingent ist inklusive, wer mehr will, wechselt in einen teureren Tarif. Apple geht beim ersten eigenen Versuch einen anderen Weg und verkauft zusätzliche KI-Nutzung als einzelnes Paket. Den Auftakt macht Logic Pro.

Intelligence Usage Packs

Seit dem aktuellen Update der Musiksoftware für den Mac gibt es im App-Menü unter „Intelligence Features“ den Eintrag „Show Usage“. Dort seht ihr, wie viel vom monatlichen Kontingent schon verbraucht ist, und eine Historie zeigt die bisherige Nutzung. Über „Buy More Usage“ gelangt ihr zum sogenannten Intelligence Usage Pack, das in den USA 49,99 US-Dollar kostet. Andere Größen oder Alternativen gibt es nicht. Aufgefallen ist die Option zuerst 9to5Mac.

Apple Creator Studio als Voraussetzung

Wer zugreifen will, braucht ein laufendes Abo von Apple Creator Studio. Angezapft wird das Zusatzguthaben erst, wenn das reguläre Monatskontingent erschöpft ist. Reste werden in den nächsten Monat übernommen, bis sie ein Jahr nach dem Kauf verfallen. Teilen lässt sich das Paket nicht, es bleibt an den Apple Account gebunden, über den es gekauft wurde. Rückerstattungen gibt es nur, wo das Gesetz sie vorschreibt.

Das Paket deckt den Logic-Assistenten ab, der auf Googles Gemini basiert und vorerst nur US-Englisch spricht. Dazu kommen die Generatoren für Bilder, Formen, Präsentationen und Sprechernotizen. Wie großzügig das Grundkontingent ausfällt, zeigt ein Beispiel: Sprechernotizen gibt es jeden Monat für mindestens 700 Folien, sofern ihr nur diese Funktion nutzt. Beim Assistenten hängt der Verbrauch dagegen davon ab, wie komplex eure Anfragen sind. Wie viel Mehrleistung die knapp 50 US-Dollar konkret bringen, lässt der Konzern offen.

Ausweitung nur eine Frage der Zeit

In den kommenden Wochen dürfte die Kaufoption auch in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro sowie Keynote, Pages und Numbers auftauchen. Deren angekündigte KI-Updates sind noch für November geplant. Angeboten werden die Pakete in acht Ländern, neben den USA unter anderem in Deutschland, Frankreich und Großbritannien. Hiesige Preise hat Cupertino noch nicht veröffentlicht. Den Verzicht auf ein weiteres Abo rechnen wir Apple durchaus an. Ein fester Preis ohne klar definierte Gegenleistung ist dagegen schwer zu verargumentieren, zumal das Creator-Studio-Abo selbst nur 12,99 Euro im Monat kostet. Mehr Transparenz wäre hier das Mindeste.

articleBody:
Walk down Pink Street in Lisbon’s Cais do Sodré and you’ll eventually find a door that looks like it has secrets. Pensão Amor building is a former brothel that has been transformed into a surprising space in Lisbon's port district.

Cais do Sodré was once the sailors’ quarter, where seamen fresh off the boats mingled with writers, fado singers, artists, prostitutes and the occasional spy. Pensão Amor takes that cast of characters and gives them a party.

The bar is a riot of velvet, red light, and cheerful mischief. On any given night, you might catch burlesque, pole dancing, live music, poetry, or theater, sometimes all in the same week.  Nobody here is trying to hide what the building used to be. They hung it on the wall.

Other surprise is upstairs. In 2023, the old brothel floors reopened as Madam’s Lodge, a 22-room hotel with a twist: every room has its own invented backstory. Screenwriter and director Roger Mor wrote each one, drawing on archival research and objects tied to the building and the neighborhood.

Illustrator Nuno Saraiva drew the characters and left his mark across the building, so even the walls seem to have opinions. Some rooms also come with pole dancing bars, strategically placed mirrors, bathtubs made for two, and minibars stocked with adult goodies.

title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

title: Open-source AI without Jensen
subtitle: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem.
